text: Notes on the used data For the calculation of the energy indicators, the Eurostat ‘Complete_Energy_Balances, NRG_BAL_C’ datasets, retrieved in March 2023, were used5. For the calculation of the GHG intensity factor, the EEA ‘Total net emissions with international aviation (EU NDC), All GHG gases (CO2 eq.), Emissions per GDP in tCO2eq. per milEUR(2015)’ dataset, retrieved in March 2024, was used6. The source for PRIMES MIX 55% Scenario, the 2020 EU Reference Scenario projections for 2030, and the updated 2020 EU Reference Scenario projections for 2030 is the PRIMES model run by the E3MLab of National Technical University of Athens (NTUA). The results of the PRIMES MIX 55% Scenario were produced for the impact assessment accompanying the Commission’s proposal for a Directive on energy efficiency (recast) in July 20217. The 2020 EU Reference Scenario projections for 2030 were published by the Commission in 20208. The updated 2020 EU Reference Scenario projections for 2030 were developed, in accordance with Article 4(5) of the EED recast. The updated version of the 2020 EU Reference Scenario, includes the following limited changes: • Historical data of energy consumption were updated, and the model was calibrated to the relevant 2021 Eurostat data. • Projections for economic growth and population were updated in line with the latest projections, used by the European Commission for the 2040 Climate Target modelling9. • International fuel prices updated to the trajectories used by the European Commission in the REPowerEU plan10 analysis. • Technology costs were updated in line with the latest projections used by the European Commission for the 2040 Climate Target modelling. 5 https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/database 6 https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/total-greenhouse-gas-emission-trends 7 https://commission.europa.eu/publications/proposals-delivering-european-green-deal_en 8 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/data-and-analysis/energy-modelling/eu-reference-scenario-2020_en 9 https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/climate-strategies-targets/2040-climate-target_en 10 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/repowereuaffordable-secure-and-sustainable-energy-europe_en

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 9 1 Introduction The successful implementation of the recast Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) is crucial for achieving the European Union's energy efficiency, clean energy transition and sustainability goals. However, translating policy objectives into concrete measures can be complex and challenging for Member States. The legislative text of the EED serves as the primary legal framework, setting out the necessary obligations, targets and timetables for Member States to follow when implementing energy efficiency measures. The guidance notes adopted by the European Commission aim to support Member States in the transposition and implementation of the EED. Good practices serve as valuable references and sources of inspiration for Member States in their efforts to design and implement effective energy efficiency measures. T his practical report thus presents exemplary initiatives in various Member States, highlighting innovative approaches, best practices, and lessons learned. By providing examples, this report helps Member States understand how concrete solutions have been used to translate legal requirements into effective and impactful energy efficiency policies. In this report, we will explore and analyse a wide range of good practices related to the different articles of the recast EED. These examples will provide Member States with practical insights on possible ways to navigate the complexities of implementation. By highlighting the successful experiences of other Member States, this report aims to inspire and enable governments to adopt and adapt these good practices, ultimately contributing to the successful implementation of the recast EED across the European Union.

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 10 2 Article 3 on the Energy Efficiency First principle 2.1 Introduction Energy efficiency first (EE1st) is a horizontal guiding principle of the European climate and energy governance. It is supposed to ensure that only the necessary amount of energy is produced and that investments in stranded assets are avoided in the pathway to achieve the climate goals. To support the application of the EE1st principle, this Annex provides some illustrative best practices. In line with Article 3(1), these best practices are grouped into policy and planning decisions. As this is a new provision for major investment decisio ns, no example can be provided yet. Within each type of decision, they are differentiated according to their sectoral scope, in line with A rticle 3(1), comprising (a) energy systems (e.g. electricity networks) and (b) non-energy sectors. 2.2 Policy decisions As suggested by the ENEFIRST project1, “implementing EE1st is not necessarily about adopting new policies: it is firstly about ensuring that the existing policies and regulations are in line with the EE1st principle.” Good practices identified across Member States provide valuable insights into the practical application of policy decisions in both energy and non-energy sectors. In electricity markets, ensuring non-discriminatory market access for demand-side flexibility has been identified as a good practice, particularly beneficial for the building, industry and transport sectors. This approach aims to remove regulatory barriers and allow demand -side resources and aggregators to participate i n the market, thereby increasing competition. Finland and Spain are notable examples where such practices have been implemented, improving market dynamics and consumer benefits.2,3 For electricity networks, the introduction of Total Expenditure (TOTEX) remuneration for network companies encourages operators to consider all possible solutions - operational and capital intensive - on an equal basis. The UK's experience with TOTEX remuneration highlights its effectiveness in promoting nonwires solutions as viable alte rnatives to traditional infrastructure investment. Similarly, performance -based regulation in the UK and Italy rewards regulated network operators for meeting specific benc hmarks, such as reducing peak demand, thereby shifting the focus to cost-effective non-wires solutions.4,5 Time-differentiated energy and network pricing , implemented in coun tries such as Spain, Bulgaria and Denmark, incentivises demandside flexibility by aligning energy prices with the marginal supply cost. This pricing strategy encourages consumers to adjust their electricity 1 Broc, Jean-Sébastien; Pató, Zsuzsanna; Mandel, Tim; Fabbri, Mariangiola; Oikonomou, Vlasis (2022): Putting Energy Efficiency First into Practice. This facilitates the integration of efficient heating solutions, including waste heat, heat pumps and renewable heat sources, thereby promoting competition between producers.8 Energy efficiency obligation schemes, which require energy companies to meet specific energy savings targets, have proved effective in France and Italy. These schemes force companies to prioritise energy efficiency measures in order to meet their targets.9 Building renovation passports , introduced in countries such as Bulgaria, France and Germany, guide building owners on the most costeffective renovation strategies. These passports suggest an optimal sequence and combination of measures to improve both the building envelope and technical systems.10 Financial incentives linked to the energy performance of buildings, as implemented in Ireland, demonstrate the importance of linking renewable energy installations to minimum energy performance standards. This ensures that investments in distributed renewable energy are complemented by fundamental improvements in the energy efficiency of buildings.11 Good practice example of EE1st application in policy decisions: Non -discriminatory market access for demand-side flexibility Facilitating market entry is crucial for nurturing competition and fostering innovation in various sectors. The EE1st principle underscores that demand -side flexibility serves as a system resource that can directly compete with conventional generation in electricity markets. This type of flexibility contributes to energy markets in real -time, offers ancillary services for maintaining grid stability, and engages in capacity markets to guarantee sufficient power supply during times of peak demand. However, despite its considerable potential, demand-side flexibility encounters regulatory hurdles, such as strict eligibility criteria, complex tendering processes and restrictive product designs. Regulation (EU) 2019/943 concerning the internal electricity market has set definitive guidelines to enable the integration of these flexible resources, both as standalone entities and through aggregation. Nevertheless, the adoption of these guidelines is progressing slowly. In numerous Member States, balancing markets and ancillary services uphold onerous technical requir ements. The smartEn 2022 Monitoring Report titled “The Implementation of the Electricity Market Design to Drive Demand-Side Flexibility,”12 contains a section dedicated to the participation of demandside flexibility resources across all electricity markets and mechanisms. The report's survey of Member States identifies France and Finland as leading examples, exhibiting satisfactory to modest enactment of legal standards for market access. In France, the capacity mechanisms are designed to be technology-neutral in terms of participation. The involvement of flexibility resources is more progressive compared to other nations, yet it remains relatively li mited when contrasted with traditional generation sources. 2.3 Planning decisions Energy planning can be understood as the process of planning investments and operating the systems for the production, distribution and use of energy in a manner that meets the energy needs of a particular region or location while contributing to social-political goals such as decarbonisation. A central component of energy planning is the quantitative analysis of energy sector trends based on cost -benefit analysis. A s pecific regulatory aspect is the realignment of the various energy networks to the shifting fuel supply. In the area of heat, electricity and gas, the development of national long -term renovation strategies stands out as good practice. These strategies provide an integrated assessment of energy supply options - including electricity, heat and gas - and technical building systems such as heating, cooling and ventilation. This approach also includes energy eff iciency and flexibility options, such as retrofitting the building envelope or using waste heat, and takes into account the wider benefits of energy effici ency. Examples of countries implementing these strategies include Spain, Belgium and Finland, which have integrated these considerations into their national planning frameworks.13,14 Local heating and cooling planning within the same sectors is another example of good practice, with countries such as Austria, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovakia and Portugal undertaking comprehensive planning efforts. These efforts are reflected in detailed assessments of efficient heating and cooling carried out by countries such as Germany, Ireland and Cyprus, which explore the potential for systemic efficiency improvements.15 In the electricity sector, the practice of increasing distribution network transparency is emerging as a noteworthy approach. By making network hosting capacity and connection options transparent, Distribution System Operators (DSOs) in countries such as the UK and Cyprus are enabling better decisions for new users on where to site new infrastructure. This not only facilitates the integration of new energy consumers and producers, but also helps to avoid or delay the need for grid expansion, thereby supporting a more efficient and flexible energy infrastructure.1617 12 https://smarten.eu/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/The_implementation_of_the_Electricity_Market_Design_2022_DIGITAL.pdf 13 European Commission (2022): Analysis of the national long-term renovation strategies. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 13 These identified good practices in planning decisions across different sectors illustrate the comprehensive and integrated approach required for effective energy planning. By considering a wide range of energy supply options, technical system upgrades and efficiency measures, these practices aim to optimise energy distribution and use. In addition, the focus on transparency and the inclusion of wider benefits in planning processes underline the importance of informed and holistic decision making in achieving sustainable energy goals. Good practice example of EE1st application in planning decisions: Integrated heating and cooling planning in Munich, Germany18,19 There are several recent and notable examples of integrated heating and cooling planning in European municipalities that demonstrate good practice in applying the EE1st principle by focusing on enduse energy efficiency in buildings, the use of renewable e nergy sources and the optimisation of existing infrastructure. Among these, Munich's Integrated Heating and Cooling Plan20 stands out as a strategic initiative in line with the city's broader ambition to reduce CO2 emissions and transition to sustainable energy. Central to Munich's strategy is the expansion of its district heating network. The plan focuses on replacing coal-fired heating plants with more sustainable options, such as large-scale heat pumps and thermal storage. Improving the energy efficiency of exi sting buildings is another key aspect. Retrofitting buildings to reduce energy demand demonstrates Munich's commitment to the EE1st principle, prioritising the reduction of energy consumption as a primary objective. Implementing Munich's plan involves overcoming challenges, in particular balancing the expansion of the heating network with environmental and urban considerations. The city is addressing these through careful planning and extensive stakeholder engagement to ensure the harmonious integration of its strategies. The evolution of Munich's strategy, underpinned by political support and multi-stakeholder collaboration, serves as an instructive example, albeit one that continues to evolve and be refined. Backed by supportive policies at various levels of government, Munich's Integrated Heating and Cooling Plan provides an insight into how urban energy planning can incorporate the EE1st principle. The effectiveness of the plan will be evaluated on an ongoing basis, positioning Munich's approach as a potentially instructive model for European municipalities seeking to integrate EE1st principles into their energy strategies, recognising that each municipality’s situation will have unique aspects and challenges. 2.4 Major investment decisions Several good practices in major investment decisions have emerged in energy systems and non - energy sectors, highlighting innovative approaches to integrating energy efficiency: 1) Holyhead Powersave Project (UK): Initiated in 1990 in Wales, this project aimed to defer the construction of a EUR 1 million substation. With an investment of EUR 500 000, which became EUR 400 000 after EU funding, the project successfully reduced peak demand by 10%, delaying the need for the substation by five years and generating savings of EUR 500 000.21 18 https://decarbcitypipes2050.eu/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Munich-CityNarratives.pdf 19 https://decarbcitypipes2050.eu/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/D3.3-HC-plan-Munich.pdf 20 https://decarbcitypipes2050.eu/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/D3.3-HC-plan-Munich.pdf 21 Rosenow, Jan; Bayer, Edith; Rososinska, Barbara; Genard, Quentin; Toporek, Marta (2016): Efficiency First: From Principle to Practice. By focusing on energy efficiency and renewable energy, the plan has succeeded in reducing consumption by 20% and ensuring security of supply by 2030.21 3) Krakow Energy Efficiency Project (Poland): In 2002, Krakow's district heating company initiated a World Bank-funded project to improve its inefficient system, leading to the creation of an efficiency-focused company. This has resulted in annual savings of around EUR 300 000 and significant reductions in energy consumption and capacity.21 4) Oakland Clean Energy Initiative (USA): Developed to replace a retiring 165 MW fossil fuel plant, the Oakland Clean Energy Initiative, launched in mid2022, prioritised demand -side resources, including energy efficiency and demand response, complemented by distributed generation and storage.11 5) Delta Project (USA): PG&E's Delta Project in California used local end-use efficiency measures to defer transmission and distribution upgrades from 1991 to 1993 and ongoing since 2013, reducing investment costs from USD 113 million to USD 75 million over 30 years and achieving significant energy savings.11 6) Central Hudson Gas & Electric's Peak Perks programme (USA): Launched in New York in 2016, the programme aimed to defer infrastructure needs in three zones for 5 -10 years. Through the use of Wi -Fi thermostats and load control switches, it achieved a load reduction of 5. MW.22 These cases highlight the transformative potential of integrating energy efficiency measures into major investment decisions, demonstrating significant financial savings and contributing to sustainability goals. Good practice example of EE1st application in major investment decisions: Brooklyn - Queens Demand Management Programme (BQDM) 23 Rising electricity load in New York's Brooklyn/Queens was identified as a risk for overloading existing infrastructure and lead to reliability concerns in 2018. Traditional approaches to relieve grid congestion would have included a new distribution substa tion, expanding an existing 345 kV switching station and constructing a sub-transmission feeder to connect the two stations at an estimated cost of USD 1 billion. Instead, the Public Service Commission (the New York State energy office) ordered Con Edison (the local utility) to look at non -traditional investments as ways to manage demand growth. 52 MW out of the required 69 MW peak demand reduction had been covered by demand reduction solutions to defer the traditional infrastructure investment for at least seven years with a USD 200 million budget in 2014. The regulator offered incentives to adopt these alternatives: a rate of return on programme cost and accelerated depreciation compared to traditional investment. The BQDM programme was part of a broader policy vision of New York state (Reforming the Energy Vision - REV) to integrate DER solutions to serve consumers reliably. The regulator played a key role by approving the least -cost option and providing incentives for the utility provider to adopt innovative solutions. The regulator extended the programme beyond the initial three-year scope, and it served as a test case for non-wire solutions across the US. 22 Chew, Brenda; Myers, Erika; Adolf, Tiger; Thomas, Ed (2018): Non -Wires Alternatives. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 15 3 Article 5 on the public sector leading on energy efficiency 3.1 Introduction The EED recast puts a specific focus on the public sector, with three interlinked Articles that define requirements and targets to be achieved by public bodies: While Article 5 defines an obligation to reduce final energy consumption and Article 6 contains a renovation obligation for public buildings (cf. chapter 4); Article 7 focuses on one of the main challenges to achieve energy efficiency as public body, i.e. the framework of public procurement (cf. chapter 5). The public sector is an important economic actor with a significant share in final energy consumption: All levels of public administration, education, health and social services, public transport, water supply and treatment as well as street lighting together account for about 30% of the energy consumption of the service sector across the EU, which equals approximately 5% of total final energy consumption. Some Member States have already incorporated sustainable energy considerations, including energy efficiency, into the ir long-term planning schemes. Furthermore, various initiatives exist at the European level as well as on national level, which include the elaboration of different forms of decarbonisation or sustainable energy plans by local authorities. Usually, energy efficiency measures are already an integral part of the planning process. Furthermore, most of the initiatives foresee some kind of quality assurance for the long-term plans as well as for the implementation procedures. Nevertheless, capacity and knowledge barriers within the public sector in many Member States may affect the identification and implementation of energy efficiency investments. Reduction of energy consumption for the public sector must also contend with other barriers24: • Difficulty of coordinating energy goals, plans and actions through different levels i.e. nationalregional-local governments and types of public organizations, complexity of establishing the baseline of energy consumption; • Difficulty in quantifying the energy efficiency performance and the improvement of buildings purchased or rented by public bodies; • Difficulty in monitoring the consumption and energy efficiency measures implemented in buildings or infrastructures owing to the lack of proper tools and the limited knowhow of technicians to use them; • Varying definitions used by public bodies and the activities they perform amongst Member States, which makes it difficult to identify organisations that need to comply with energy efficiency obligations. At the level of the Members States as a whole, a presentation of the chosen policy mix at the different levels of the public sector is also required as part of the revision of the integrated national energy and climate plan, which is regulated by Article 14(2) of the Governance Regulation25. 24 Gynther, L. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 16 3.2 Supporting public sector organisations to implement energy management practices 26 Supporting public bodies in the uptake of energy efficiency improvement measures is critical because an important barrier to achieving renovations by public bodies is the lack of capacity to conduct the process of renovations. The example from Ireland, described below, demonstrates how targeted support to public sector organisations can help overcome barriers resulting from lack of skills, knowledge and expertise of building managers / maintenance staff on energy renovations while also enabling the monitoring, reporting, and verification of energy efficiency measures. Public bodies in Ireland have been mandated with becoming Net Zero no later than in 2050. Milestone targets have been set to reduce energy related carbon emissions by 51% and improve energy efficiency by 33% by 2020 and by 50% by 2030. The Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI)’s Public Sector Energy Progamme (PSEP) supports public sector organisations of all scales on the effective implementation of energy management practices and the ongoing monitoring of these practices. PSEP tailors the support to the organisation. SEAI support includes tools such as the Energy Management Action Plan, training, for example, on Energy Efficient Design and Energy Management System (EnMS) ISO 50001, support for project development process and linking to project assistance grants, as well as advice to integrate energy management into the general management of public sector organisations. Additionally, the SEAI offers a suite of integrated support measures to help public bodies fulfil their legal obligation to report energy performance data through the public sector energy monitoring and reporting system. Although a separate evaluation of PSEP cannot be found in the public domain, the SEAI’s Annual Report 2021 on Public Sector Energy Efficiency Performance indicates that the combined energy savings in 2020 of the public bodies and schools stood at 4 576 GWh of primary energy. This amount is equivalent to a 34.1% improvement compared to what the business -as-usual energy consumption would have been had these organisations maintained their baseline efficiency levels. This is the primary indicator used for track ing the sector’s performance against the 33% energy efficiency target for 2020. Based on 2020 data, a 33% improvement would be equivalent to 4 569 GWh of primary energy savings. The 4 576 GWh of annual energy savings for 2020 were equivalent to 848 000 tonnes of annual CO₂ savings and EUR 298 million of energy spend savings. 3.3 Monitoring and verification platform for the systematic recording and evaluation of energy efficiency27 Article 5 requires Member States to ensure that the total final energy consumption of all public bodies combined is reduced by at least 1. 9% each year, when compared to the year 2021. This would require monitoring and verification (M&V) schemes that enable the quantification of the EE performance and support verification of improvements of EE measures. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 17 schemes can incorporate and support the monitoring of achievements against national energy efficiency regulations/goals. Croatia has established an M&V scheme in the form of an IT -tool called System for Monitoring, Measurement and Verification of Energy Savings (SMIV) in line with the Croatian National Energy Efficiency Action. The SMIV involves the participation of parties at all levels (local, regional, national) across the public sector, the household sector, the industry sector and the transport sector, and is used to calculate energy savings in three main sectors: building, industry, and transport. The SMIV specifically reports on the energy and cost savings from energy renovation programmes for public buildings. The SMIV began as a project developed in cooperation with GIZ and subsequently became the official national M&V tool through the Croatian Energy Efficiency Act of 2014. With this tool, Croatia is reporting energy savings as required in the EED. The tool is now hosted in the Croatian Ministry of Economy which is responsible for energy efficiency targets and the implementation of the EED through close collaboration with the Ministry of Construction and Spatial Planning (responsible for building codes, energy audits and other related to EPBD), the Ministry of Environment (responsible for public procurement), the Ministry of Transport (responsible for measures in transport), and other ministries. It incorporates the National Energy Efficiency Action Plan (NEEAP), Regional and Local Energy Efficiency Action Plans and planning instruments. All energy efficiency measures undertaken must be entered in the SMIV. The SMIV calculates energy savings using dominantly deemed savings or engineering estimates. This allows all users to generate reports, plans and calculations of their energy savings under a unified methodology. The measured energy savings are verified through algorithms in SMIV. Targets for each measure in SMIV are related to those same measures planned through the NEEAP. Documentation proving the energy savings must be uploaded in SMIV for verification by the National Energy Efficiency Authority. Data con tained in SMIV is used for many energy savings calculations, analysis and the continuous overview of achieved national energy efficiency targets. A key feature of the SMIV is that it is based on the bottom -up methodology involving several different energy efficiency measures such as building renovation, replacement of housing appliances, boiler replacement, eco -driving, etc. The bottom -up monitoring procedure and the methodology were developed in cooperation with many relevant institutions and were built upon the already existing rulebook. They were officially proposed and then adopted by the Minister of Economy. In case an end user wants to calculate the achieved energy savings for an energy efficiency measure that is not mentioned in the Rulebook, the new measure has to be proposed to the National Energy Efficiency Authority, which then has to approve the methodology or the new measure. The necessary data for the monitoring and implementation of energy efficiency measures in different sectors comes from paid subsidies. In other words, the institution providing the incentives is obligated to enter energy savings into SMIV. The National Energy Efficiency Authority is responsible for the data collection, analysis and reporting of achieved energy savings in all sectors of energy consumption. It also governs, maintains and continuously improves SMIV processes. The Authority is part of the Croatian Institution Centre for Monitoring Business Activities in the Energy Sector and Investments and was founded by Ministry of Economy in line with the Energy Efficiency Act.

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 18 3.4 Energy Efficiency Agreement for Municipalities28 This is a good practice example that addresses various aspects relevant for the implementation of Articles 5, 6, and 7. Since the 1990s, Energy Efficiency Agreements, chosen in cooperation by the National Government and industrial/municipal associations have been a primary tool to improve the efficient use of energy in Finland. The Energy Efficiency Agreement for Municipal Sector is an agreement between the Ministry of Employment and the Economy, the Energy Authority and the Association of Finnish Local and Regional Authorities on improving the efficient use of energy in the municipal sector. Participants include municipalities, cities and joint municipal authorities who sign their own Energy Efficiency Agreement. It is worth noting that the rental housing properties of municipalities are covered under the Energy Efficiency Agreement for the Property Sector. The current agreement period of the Municipalities’ Energy Efficiency Agreement spans from 2017 to 2025 and is divided into two terms: term 2017 – 2020 and term 2021 – 2025. Participation in the agreement is voluntary. A participant is required to set an indicative energy savings target of at least 7.5% for 2017 – 2025 and an intermediate target of 4% for 2020. A participant that has participated in the agreement period of 2008 – 2016 and wants to use energy savings from 2014 – 2016 is required to set an indicative energy savings target of at least 10.5% for 2014 – 2025 and an intermediate target of 7% for 2020. A participant is also required to target energy efficiency as one of the criteria in all public procurements. During the competitive tendering stage of procurements that are significant in terms of energy efficiency, bidders are required to provide suffici ent energy efficiency data on a procurement entity, appliance or system, either as a minimum requirement or a comparison criterion. Finally, the participant is required to draw up or update an action plan that takes the needs and views of the local residents into account, where possible. 3.5 Promising technical solutions for final energy consumption reduction in the public sector 3.5.1 Waste disposal - Collection of landfill gas To reduce the climate impact of landfilled organic material, the collection of landfill gas is important. This gas has a similar composition to fermentation gas and can be used in generators for small scale energy production. As gas production is decreasing over time, gas collection at some point becomes uneconomical. Therefore, and due to leakages, only a maximum 50% gas collection rate can be reached. The gas can be used onsite in combustion engines with electric generators to reduce energy consumption of landfills or feed heat into a district heating system. 28 Energy Efficiency Agreements (Undated). In regions with low availability of freshwater, it must be transported further using more energy. Irrigation is a significant factor in many European regions and makes up 70% of the worldwide freshwater demand. (ABB, 2021)31 • In general, 80 to 85% of the energy demand of water extraction and transportation can be attributed to water pumps. • Many of the electric motors used in existing water distribution systems have an energy efficiency class of IE 1 to IE 3. Each step up in efficiency class corresponds to a 20% reduction of losses. High-efficiency motors with an IE class of up to 5 are available. • Even more significant is the energy saving potential by correct dimensioning and implementing efficient control strategies for partial-load operation. • Mechanical reduction of the flow rate by obstructing the flow results in large energy losses. • Cyclic operation of electric motors, where the motor is periodically switched on and off, is more efficient, though not feasible for many applications and reduc ing the life expectancy of the motor. • Therefore, the option that significantly reduces energy demand is the use of variable speed motors. These motors are electronically controlled and can operate over a wide power range. 31 ABB, (2021), White Paper, Energieeffizienz als Herausforderung bei Wasserversorgern und Abwasserbetrieben, ABB

(ABB, 2021)35 State-of-the-art desalination plants are functioning on the reverse-osmosis principle, which is using semi-permeable membranes and high-pressure pumps to separate freshwater from brine. Back in the 1970s, when the technology started to be commercialised, sometimes well over 20 kWh were required to desalinate one cubic meter of water. These can either be shaped as water turbines, but preferably as so called “work exchangers” or “pressure exchangers” (PX). These devices use the pressurised brine directly to pressurize the new feed-saltwater. Desalination plants equipped with pressure exchangers have an energy demand as low as 60% of plants equipped with Francis-turbines. To reach the highest efficiency in heat recovery, decentrali sed solutions in houses are necessary. Central heat recovery systems in large sewers or after WWTPs benefit from stable water flow and have better economic viability. The effect of wastewater-cooling on decomposition processes needs to be studied but seems to be negligible (Frijns et al., 2012)38. 3.5.3 Electrification of public transport and public service fleets Electric vehicles are significantly more energy efficient for locomotion compared to vehicles with internal combustion engines. Conventional combustion engine vehicle supply systems transform a maximum of 37% of the primary energy input into mechanical power. Electric vehicle systems can, on the one hand, be powered by renewable energy, but on the other hand use this energy much more efficiently, with a well-to-wheel efficiency of up to 72%. (Albatayneh et al., 2020)39 This is due to the high losses of fossil fuels energy during processing, as well as to the high efficiency of electric drivetrains. Next to the significant impact on reducing GHG -Emissions, the overall energy consumption of electric vehicles is also much lower. Battery electric vehicles are significantly more efficient than conventional drive and hybrid vehicles. If only the energy consumption during their operation is considered, EVs consume 30% of the energy compared to similar ICV. (Braun & Rid, 2017)40 In the context of public infrastructure, several applications can be identified, to be converted to battery electric propulsion. 3.5.3.1 Public Transport Although a large share of public transport is already running electric in many EU countries, this is by far not a standard. The described improvement of electric propulsion makes it possible and even viable in many cases to replace many busses with electric ones. According to Say et al., (2024)41 who did a total-cost-of-ownership (TCO) analysis on the economies of electric busses, the most significant economic factors are purchase, maint enance and energy costs. Generally, EVs have similar maintenance but higher investment costs. As of 2022, the TCO of electric busses with low power charging capabilities is already similar to average diesel busses. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 24 3.5.3.2 Municipal vehicle fleet Especially in cities, many small vehicles are used to support maintenance tasks. Most of these vehicles only travel small distances and can be charged overnight at a depot. The same goes for municipal police vehicles, which are typically deployed in a relatively small area with short driving distances and large shares of idling hours. Besides being more energy efficient, they fit better in future city concepts and park landscaping by emitting no exhaust fumes and less noise. This makes them significantly less invasive in spaces where people travel by foot or bike.42 3.5.3.3 Garbage collection Due to the intensive use and predictable routes, there is a high potential to replace garbage collection vehicles with electric alternatives. Garbage collectio n vehicles spend a large amount of time idling, providing power for garbage compression or mobile cranes, which could also be powered by electric hydraulic pumps. Exhaust and noise pollution is also reduced by transitioning to electric systems. The cities of Vienna 43 and Copenhagen44 have already started using electric garbage collection vehicles in daily practice. 3.5.4 Heating and cooling in public transport An easily underestimated factor in the operation of public transport vehicles is the energy demand for auxiliary devices, especially for air conditioning. Especially during wintertime, non -traction energy needs are almost as high as traction energy needs, which can also be attributed to situations were a bus is stationary but maintains a specific interior climate. In Figure 5, it can also be observed that the share of auxiliary energy consumption rises, when busses move slowly, e.g. due to slow traffic. 42 A few case studies for the use of small-size electric vehicles used by municipalities are shown here: https://www.alke.com/company/case - studies 43 https://smartcity.wien.gv.at/en/electic-powered-waste-collection-vehicle/ 44 https://group.vattenfall.com/press-and-media/newsroom/2023/silent-revolution-as-copenhagens-rubbish-trucks-goes-electric

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 26 Using CO2 heat pumps, energy demand for heating can be reduced by up to 60%. The energy source is typically the ambient air but can also be used for cooling power electronics or other waste heat from the powertrain. This technology can be used not only for busses, but for all means of public transport. Recent developments for trans-critical CO2 vapor injection heat pumps in the electric car manufacturing market have made this technology widely available, easy to implement as well as affordable.45 3.5.5 Heat pump variations Heat pumps are a technologically mature alternative to conventional heating and cooling systems. Although the exact efficiency values are strongly dependent on environmental factors such as source temperature and heat distribution system, they are in general significantly more efficient than alternative systems. Typically, low temperature gradients and large surface areas are used to optimise efficiency. As a small example, a typical primary school in Austria is presented. For simplicity, only the heating demand is considered. Depending the investment costs and energy prices, heat pumps reach financial parity with most other technologies well within th eir operational lifetime. New technologies make it possible to use heat pumps for a wide range of applications. High temperature heat pumps For replacing conventional heating systems with as minimal an impact on the existing heat distribution system as possible, it is advisable to maintain similar temperature levels. Especially the generation of hot service water, requires high temperatures, to meet consumer comfortand hygiene requirements. In low temperature heating systems, this is often achieved using electric heating coils, which heat water purely electric. Especially for small-scale applications, this is a very simple and low-investment possibility.46 45 An example for the use of CO2 heat pumps is presented here: https://r744.com/german -cities-opting-for-hydrogen-buses-with-co2-heatpumps/ 46 A detailed description of the technology can be found here: https://www.dw.com/en/expensive -gas-prices-have-many-home-owners-turn-torenewable-energy-sources-for-heating/a-63779877

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 27 Existing high temperature distribution systems can in many cases be used for low temperature heat supply systems. Especially after façade renovations and a corresponding decrease in heating load, radiators with low temperatures are sufficient for heating. In case of additional heat loads, the high temperature cycle of the heat pump can be used as a booster, to increase heating water temperature. However, the overall heating efficiency decreases compared to low temperature situations. With the development of high-quality building envelopes, heating loads have been decreasing over the last years. Especially newly constructed buildings in Central Europe have a very low demand for heating energy and a slightly increased demand for hot water. Cooling heat pumps Heat pumps using ground-based energy sources like geothermal piles or groundwater operate in a temperature range which is optimal for reversing energy flow during summertime. Depending on the temperature of the energy source, it may be used directly with heat-exchangers in large-area cooling or using the heat pump for creating very low temperature fluid to dehumidify or cool fresh air in a ventilation system. The principle is very similar to other compression chillers, with the main difference being the coo ling source and cooling distribution. Heat pumps often use geothermal sources or groundwater as an environmental source, which provide high efficiencies compared to ambient air heat pumps. One of the most important aspects of heat pumps is the possibility of cooling large thermal masses within a building, which act as a thermal storage. This way, buildings won't heat up as quickly during the day and lower peak loads will be demanded from the heat pump. As maximum cooling loads and maximum PV -generation coincide with each other, these two technologies complement each other and can significantly reduce energy consumption from the electric grid. 3.5.5.1 Thermal energy recovery in buildings Heat from wastewater and exhaust air is an increasingly utilised energy source. It can be done either via heat exchangers, which can only recover a portion of the thermal energy, or via heat pumps, which can recover a significantly higher amount of energy. The viability of this concept depends on the availability of large waste energy flows and the economic feasibility of the chosen solution. One example is to adapt existing sewage mains with heat exchangers to cool down warm wastewater. Most of this energy is currently being dissipated into the environment on the way to the wastewater treatment plant . Using heat -pumps and speciali sed sewer-heat exchangers, this reliable temperature gradient can be utilised to heat buildings or feed into low temperature district heating systems. (Averfalk et al., 2021)47 To utilise the highest temperatures and therefore achieve the highest possible efficiency, systems have been developed which recuperate waste-heat directly within the building using simple bufferstorage tanks with an integrated heat exchanger.48 47 Averfalk et al., (2021), Low-Temperature District Heating Implementation Guidebook, International Energy Agency technology collaboration program on district heating and cooling, Fraunhofer Verlag 48 A few examples for the practical application of this technology are given in the following sources: https://www.nn.de/region/neumarkt/energie-aus-abwasser-huber-se-beheizt-das-haus-der-bayerischen-geschichte-in-regensburg1.13448284; https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/nov/08/how-the-dutch-went-down-the-toilet-looking-for-heat-sewage

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 29 4 Article 6 on the exemplary role of public bodies' buildings 4.1 Introduction Renovating public buildings larger than 250 m2 to nearly zero-energy buildings (NEZB) or zero emission buildings ( ZEB) standard will involve thousands of public bodies and pose significant coordination challenges for public bodies spread across entire national territories. The vast majority of public bodies across the EU are going to be involved in some manner , with practical, organisational and budgetary implications . Furthermore, in order to reliably and efficiently meet the obligation to renovate, data need to be collected and exchanged between different bodies. 4.2 Financing the renovation of social housing49 It is possible to carry out renovations of social housing efficiently and effectively leveraging external finance and implementation support . The case of Dublin City Council, described below , demonstrates how the use of new business models and financing options , specifically Energy Service Companies (ESCOs), can help overcome financing barriers . This initiative also shows how the complexity of these renovations can be handled optimally. The Dublin City Council (DCC) aimed to upgrade its social housing stock to be more energy efficient, with funding from the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI). The upgrade is being done under a programme called the Energy Efficiency Fabric Upgrade Programme , and has supported the delivery of DCC’s target of 33% reduction in emissions by 2020. Within this programme, the DDC targeted Cromcastle Court, consisting of eight four-storey blocks with a total of 128 apartments, all of them owned by the DCC. Prior to renovation, heating and hot water were provided by a communal heating system via gas boilers located in a boiler room (one for each block). Being a relatively old system, it gave residents no control over the heating in their individual apartments. The renovation involved a number of different actions. First of all, the replacement of the gas boilers with two split heat pumps and a remote access control system; this allows the DCC to log in to the heating management systems and check or change the temperature in each building. Then, a number of other improvements exploited various energy savings opportunities: apartment-level control systems ( that allow each resident to control their heating independently), replacement of domestic hot water tanks with new fast -recovery tanks, and installation of double-glazed windows. The renovation, led by DCC’s Housing Department, involved a tender for an Energy Services Contract for 7.5 years, with an ESCO that would install, finance, operate and maintain the equipment for the agreed period of time. The ESCO paid the energy bills, in exchange for payments based on the building’s historic energy use. The cost of the upgrade, as ascertained from the value of the contract awarded by the DCC, was EUR 13 860 000 excluding VAT. The renovation was predicted to deliver savings of EUR 834 700 on heating cost and maintenance over 10 years. 49 CODEMA (2013). Dublin City Council’s Fabric Upgrade Programme. The upgrades are estimated to have resulted in savings of 508 200 MWh valued at EUR 46.4 million during this period. 4.3 Building the i nventory of local, regional and national public buildings50 Below, we present the approach of the Portuguese Energy Agency (ADENE) and how it dealt with data availability. Its approach shows how the effects of energy improvements can be quantified , how data on regional renovation measures can be monitored, reported and verified by national governments and lastly, how it can be put together in a single data repository. A key element of success is the training provided to building managers and maintenance staff concerning energy renovations. ADENE has set up a database for EPCs of all types of buildings including the EPCs of buildings owned and occupied by public entities and frequently visited by the public which have a useful interior floor area exceeding 250 m2. EPCs became mandatory for the construction, purchase or lease process of all residential and service buildings, whether new, refurbished or existing under the Buildings Energy Certification System (SCE) that was implemented in Portugal through the DecreeLaw 78/2006. Accredited qualified experts or companies recognised by ADENE have access to the database and enter the EPC information. The database is open to the public and allows anyone to search for an EPC based on the address, the building's property data, as well as through the number of the energy certificate. ADENE also publishes statistics based on the data stored in the database, aiming to characterise different aspects related to the energy performance of the building stock. The statistics provide trends and comparisons in number of EPCs by year, by energy efficiency rating, by region, by district, by county and even by building classification of new buildings, renovated buildings and existing buildings. The statistics are automatically generated on the website on a daily basis. Municipal authorities and other local and regional authorities are required by legislation (Decree - Law no. 101-D/2020, of 07 December) to obtain and make available energy certificates for new or rehabilitated residential, and commercial and service buildin gs owned by the public authorities. Public authorities are required to submit annually the energy consumption data, results of the implementation of the building maintenance plan, and the documentation related to the technical systems installed in the building in the EPC portal. The EPC database connects with the National Institute of Statistics (INE) and the electricity provider, Energias de Portugal (EDP), databases. Where required, depending on the potential energy savings within a single project, RenoWatt groups multiple buildings to achieve an adequate size for the EPC, diversifying the risk for financiers, and reduce transaction costs. The buildings may belong to a single public body or to multiple public bodies. The technical assistance provided by RenoWatt is free for the municipalities, local and regional authorities, as well as public or private entities acting on behalf of local and/or regional authorities. Renowatt was launched in 2014 by the Groupement de Redéploiement Economique Liège (GRE - Liège) and started with an initial capitalisation of EUR 265m from the ELENA programme (a joint initiative of the EU and European Investment Bank), Cassa Despositi e Prestiti, and Deutsche Bank. Between 2014 and 2017, in its pilot phase in the Liège area, RenoWatt enabled the renovation of 136 buildings involving 12 local authorities throug h five EPCs that included maintenance and amounted to EUR 59 million. This resulted in 33% energy savings, a reduction of 7 545 t CO2/year, a mobilization of 322 direct jobs and 780 indirect jobs. Additi onally, a leverage factor of 29.2 was achieved across the five EPCs. In 2018, the project was extended to the whole of Wallonia. Since then, 113 public authorities have used the central purchasing support of RenoWatt and buildings for a total area of 650 000 m2 were renovated. A ‘delegated mission’ of the Walloon Government since June 2022, RenoWatt is now managed by the specialist company B.E.FIN, which is 51% owned by the Walloon Government and 49% by SRIW Environnement, a private equity and venture capital firm. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 33 4.5 Financing the renovation of public buildings54 This example shows how local authorities can be supported in using national and European financial support programmes for their renovat ions. Additionally, it shows how energyrelated skills and knowledge can be increased in (local) administrations . Lastly, this example also shows how new business and financing models, such as ESE, can be implemented. In 2020, Greece instituted “ELECTRA”, a programme with a budget of EUR 640 million for the period 2020-2026, to improve the energy efficiency of the public buildings through interventions related to the use of each building as well as heating, cooling, ventilation, lighting etc. Local administrative bodies, public enterprises, organisations and legal entities financed from the national budget are eligible to apply for support from the programme. The energy upgrade should concern the whole building and not parts of it, as well as a "group" of buildings of the same body in one application. Buildings included in the programme will be classified at least in energy efficiency level B after the interventions, in accordance with the current Building Energy Efficiency Regulation (CENAK). Criteria for inclusion of projects include but are not limited to the following: • The energy upgrade should concern the whole building and not parts of it, as well as a group of buildings of the same body in one application, • The operations should concern a useful area of more than 500 m² per application, and • Projects should be economically viable. This programme runs during the period 2020 - 2026 under the control of the Ministry of Environment and Energy and is funded by borrowings from the European Investment Bank's (EIB) Consignments and Loans Fund. The financing of the projects that will be included in "ELECTRA" is partly carried out through investment loans supervised by the Technical Support Instrument55 (TSI) and concluded through loan agreements between the beneficiary entities and the Fund. The loans are serviced from an account set up in the TSI for the needs of the programme and financed by the Public Investment Programme of the Ministry of Environment. The remaining funding may come from the general government's own resources or from financing by Energy Service Companies or third parties through Energy Performance Contracts. The calls for applications for inclusion in the programme define and specify the duration and procedure of the submission, the forms and supporting documents required, the analysis of the criteria, the prioritisation of needs, the required own participation of the beneficiary entities and their obligations, the term s and conditions for granting Investment Loans by the CCS, etc. Applications are evaluated by the Directorate of Energy Policies and Energy Efficiency of the Ministry of Environment and Energy, which recommends to the Minister of Environment and Energy the issuance of a Decision for the inclusion of the project in the programme. After the issuance of the Project Completion Decision, the beneficiary entity has the obligation to ensure the operation and maintenance of the building for 5 years, to appoint an energy manager, and to implement an energy management system. 54 YPEN (2020). text: Fraunhofer ISI | 35 5 Article 7 on public procurement 5.1 Introduction The objective of Article 7 is to establish high energy efficiency performance as a criterion in public procurement. Many government jurisdictions in Member States are adopting policies that require or encourage the procurement of energy efficient products by contracting authorities and contracting entities. However, they often face a range of technical and financial barriers .56 This chapter presents a series of good practices which will support Member States in their implementation of Article 7. Good practices presented in this chapter concern some organisational aspect of public procurement as well as specifics groups of goods, works and buildings. 5.2 Public Procurement Expertise Centre57 PIANOo, set up in 2005, started out as a knowledge network for government procurement officers and contracting authorities in the Netherlands. The name “ PIANOo” stands for Professional and Innovative Tendering, Network for Government Contracting Authorities. Specifically, it was set up to professionalise procurement and tendering in all government departments, with a view to improving efficiency and compliance with procurement rules. Professional procurement can contribute to successful policy and offers value for taxpayers' money. Since 1 January 2017, PIANOo is part of the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO.nl). Netherlands Enterpri se Agency (RVO.nl) is part of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy. PIANOo brings experts in specific areas together, pools knowledge and experience and provides advice. It also fosters dialogue between government contracting authorities and private sector companies. PIANOo works for and with a network of around 3 500 public procurement and tendering professionals, municipalities, provinces, national government and other contracting authorities. It provides guidelines, manuals, best practices, an online procurement forum and it organizes workshops. PIANOo has also developed “TenderNed”, which is the Dutch government's online tendering system. All Dutch authorities are obliged to publish their national and European tenders on TenderNed's announcement platform, so businesses can access all public notices from a single webpage. The Dutch government procures around EUR 73 billion worth of work, services and supplies every year, all of that processed through PIANOo. 56 Gynther, L. (2016). The project provided direct training to 800 potential facilitators and developed facilitation materials in nine languages. These materials include a project database of over 50 good practices, a guide to the typical roles and responsibilities of energy performance contracting facilitators, and training modules. The trained specialists can now act as multipliers for the ESC concept in their regions. In addition, the project demonstrated the importance of this local assistance by implementing 27 pilot projects that triggered almost EUR 27 million of total investments in energy efficiency. 5.4 RE:FIT programme and Energy Performance contracting59 Supported by the European Local Energy Assistance (ELENA) programme, RE:FIT is a large -scale retrofit programme for public buildings in London, delivered through Energy Performance Contracting (EnPC). The programme has developed a framework contract to simplify EnPC procurement by providing pre-negotiated, European Union compliant contracts that can be used with a group of pre-qualified ESCOs for the design and implementation of energy saving measures. The framework contract helped overcome the lack of energy experts / personnel qualified on how to include EE criteria in procurement processes (helpdesk, technical assistance). The use of new business models and financing options in procurement processes also enabled the financing of long-term / high investment energy efficiency measures. The provision of EU-compliant contracts helped to overcome the skills gap at procurer level and to implement EnPC procurement. The tariff of points included bonuses for use of buses with low nitrogen oxide emissions and low noise levels (unde r "quality of bus fleet"), for various certified quality criteria and for a certified environment protection programme (under "operator's quality and environmental management"). Despite Concordia submitting the lowest tender, the contract was awarded to HKL, the city of Helsinki's own operator, which achieved a higher overall score due to bonus points for low emissions and noise levels. The ECJ held that in the contracting authority’s omission in the invitation to tender to determine the period in respect of which tenderers had to state in their tenders the amount of electricity from renewable energy sources which they could supply could be an infringement of the principles of equal treatment and transparency were it to transpire that that omission made it difficult or even impossible for tenderers to know the exact scope of the criterion in question and thus to be able to interpret it in the same way. In that case, the contracting authority was also not able to verify the criterion effectively. 5.8 Sustainable public procurement of LED lighting for a multistorey underground car park65 Cambridge City Council identified the potential for significant cost savings by replacing the lighting in one of its multi-storey car parks. The car park operates 24 hours a day throughout the year and was previously lit by over 200 metal halide light s rated at 150 W. An Electrical Design Consultant was employed to review the system and draw up a specification to replace it with LED lighting technology. Tenders were invited following a market engagement exercise, using award criteria of p rice, recycling and re -use, e nergy savings (including energy usage in watts and energy savings (%) compared with the traditional style lights), robustness, and warranty period. The successful bidder provided a high-quality LED lighting solution, good installation service and competitive pricing – the cost of GBP 77 100 represented a 35% saving against the initial budget. 5.9 Using technical specifications and award criteria for circular procurement66 In 2017, the Dutch Ministry of Defence (MODNL) procured towels and overalls, with the requirement that the goods contained at least 10% recycled post -consumer textile fibres. Suppliers were required to demonstrate this through microscopic testing that involved testing the fibre length, the quantity of damaged fibres and the kind of fibres. The award criteria recognised and awarded those offers that significantly exceeded the technical specifications (that is, achieved over 30% or 50% recycled content). The 100 000 towels purchased by the MODNL contained 36% recycled postconsumer textiles fibres, and the overalls contained 14% recycled post-consumer textiles fibres. Although the use of recycled post-consumer materials in new products r esulted in a 25% price increase compared to the previous contract, the contracts resulted in savings of 15 252 kg of cotton, 68 880 kg of CO 2, 23 520 MJ of energy, and over 233 million litres of water. A key learning here was that the usual timeline from publishing the contract to closure is too short for the market to investigate new or different production methods. It is important to give the market a reasonable period of time to respond to tender requests for information. 65 www.smart-spp.eu/fileadmin/template/projects/smart_spp/files/Case_studies/EN_ESPO_SMARTSPP_Case -Studies.pdf. 66 European Commission, Public Procurement for a Circular Economy - Good practice and guidance (2017). The city included GPP-criteria in the tender specifications, indicating a minimum of 20% of renewable energy and decided to go for the most economically advantageous procedure instead of the lowest price as only award criterion, allowing that 10% of the award points would go to the bidder with the greenest electricity offer. The procedure was more successful than anticipated with a 100% green electricity supply by the winning bidder. The choice to include GPP criteria instead of the lowest price as the only award criterion allowed savings of 1 333.85 tonnes of CO 2 on an annual basis and of 385 tonnes of oil equivalent of renewable energy triggered and an investment of EUR 193 500. 5.11 Sustainable procurement of office supplies68 In 2013, the City of Ghent tendered a four-year framework contract for paper and office supplies. All products in the tender included green criteria and technical specifications. Some of the green specifications included the following: • Remanufactured toners and cartridges (from original once used cartridges); • Paper: Preference for 100% post -consumer recycled paper. When not available for a given product, preference was given to a mixture of recycled paper and paper made from fibres from responsibly managed forests, demonstrated on the basis of the FSC, PEFC, or equivalent labels. Unbleached, totally chlorine -free (TCF) or elementary chlorine -free (ECF) paper was also required; • Exclusion of polyvinyl chloride (PVC), for example, from self-adhesives and transparent folders. Such products were required to be produced from polypropylene (PP); • Preference given to reusable or refillable products; • Water based inks for markers, for example. Contract performance clauses included a requirement for a reduction in deliveries by 85% (from daily to once or twice a month). Extra points were also awarded for greener solutions, which resulted in sustainable packaging options offered in tenders. Besides lowering the environmental impacts from pulp and paper production for paper consumables, the tender achieved lower CO 2 emissions from the decrease in delivery frequency and new packaging options. 5.12 Life-cycle costing in vehicles procurement69 The Ville de Niort in France included LCC (life-cycle costing) in its car procurement strategy. Additionally, Hungarian contracting authorities focus mainly on the initial purchasing price in procurement and do not consider any other cost elements i n their evaluation framework. The Hungarian Public Procurement Authority established a "Green Competence Centre". This Centre develop s competences to educate all market players on best practices, business solutions, financing opportunities (e.g. conferences, information on website, policy papers, workshops, etc.). Centr e staff also teach the options of applying sustainability aspects in public procurement procedures within the framework of university training. The Public Procurement Authority has created a sustainability microsite, which provides information and guides on environmental, social and innovative public procurements published in Hungary and abroad, containing good practice as well as Hungarian and international court decisions and jurisprudence. 5.14 Joint procurement of electric vehicle charging points71 To coordinate different policy choices and to boost the use of electric vehicles in the region, the City of Rotterdam, with the co-operation of The Metropolitan Region of Rotterdam and The Hague (MRDH – region), decided to also enable 16 surrounding other municipalities within the region to use the contract for procurement of charging infrastructure. Using an e -purchasing system and a joint distribution centre, the number of goods delivered to municipal facilities in Växjö have decreased by as much as 80%. An optimis ed delivery plan with predetermined routes inform the facilities in advance when to expect deliveries, which helps them to plan their work and resources and also saves time. The pilot was part of the Public Administration Procurement Innovation to Reach Ultimat e Sustainability (PAPIRUS) project which was funde d by European Union CIP Entrepreneurship and Innovation Programme . The tender was divided into three lots in order to make the participation of small and medium - sized enterprises easier: • Lot one: Integral façade solution to reduce energy losses through the building’s vertical opaque envelope; • Lot two: Partial roof solution to reduce energy losses at roof level (inner leaf); and • Lot three: Reduced solar gains in summer and increased solar gains in winter through windows. The contract was awarded based on the most economically advantageous tender, weighted according to energy efficiency, sustainability, installation and maintenance as well as economic criteria. The energy efficiency criteria comprised the following sub-award criteria: • Thermal transmittance coefficient (U-value): The aim of this criterion was to assess the capacity of the proposed innovative product or system to reduce energy losses. The minimum proposed thermal transmittance value received the maximum score, while values equal to the maximum value allowed (which differed according to the lot) were awarded zero. The rest of the values were then scored proportionally using a mathematical formula. • Thermal bridges (only applicable to ‘façade’ and ‘roof’ lots): This criterion evaluated the capacity of innovative solutions to reduce thermal bridges. Maximum points were awarded to those solutions with complete continuity of the insulation layer and good treatment of special joints. • Capacity of windows to reduce solar gains and to increase them in winter (only applicable to ‘windows’ lot): this evalua ted the proposed window systems' ability to reduce solar gains in summer while increasing them in winter. Maximum points were awarded to systems where heating and cooling demands were reduced by more than 20% compared to standard windows. The total number of submitted and accepted bids was three, all of which were for lot three. The procurement was declared void for the first two lots because no bids were received. The purchase of the solutions for lots one and two (façade and roof) were subsequently included as part of a separate tender to contract the renovation works. The requirements were formulated in a way which took into account the experiences learnt through the first round of procurement (for the solutions/products). The tender for Lot three was awarded in July 2015 and the subsequent renovation works were carried out between April and August 2016.

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 43 6 Article 8 on energy savings obligations, Article 9 on the energy efficiency obligation schemes , Article 10 on the alternative policy measures and A NNEX V on the common methods and principles for their calculation 6.1 Introduction The EED recast brings several changes and clarifications to the EED energy savings obligation. This chapter presents a series of good practices which will support Member States in their implementation of Article s 8, 9 and 10. Good practices presented in this chapter concern both Energy Efficiency Obligation Schemes, as well as alternative measures, they cover measures in buildings, transport, taxation, as well as those related to ETS . Particular attention is given to the monitoring and verification of savings. 6.2 Policy measures contributing to tackle energy poverty 6.2.1 Energy efficiency obligation schemes (Article 9) Some Energy Efficiency Obligation Schemes ( EEOSs) have already had specific goals related to energy poverty alleviation and set targets or sub-targets to be achieved within particular groups. Until 2020, Austria applied an uplift factor of 1.5 to energy savings from actions carried out in households affected by energy poverty, i.e. energy savings are multiplied by a factor of 1.5 when calculating compliance with obligated parties’ targets. Similarly, Greece applies a bonus of 40% (i.e. uplift factor of 1.4) to energy savings from actions tackling energy poverty. However, the results obtained until 2020 showed that relying on a bonus factor only was not successful in achieving a significant share of energy savings in the ‘energy poverty’ scope. The same has been observed in Croatia (see details about the Croatian EEOS below). In France, specific programme s targeting low income households have been in place since 2010 (e.g. "Habiter Mieux"/Living Better programme, now replaced with “MaPrimeRénov Sérénité”). Until 2016, these programmes were rewarded with White Certificates (in kWh cumac) based on a fix rate of kWh cumac per euro invested by obligated parties in these programmes (at a higher price than White Certificates on the market). These ‘bonus’ White Certificates were not reported to the EED energy savings obligation. In 201 6, France established a sub -target for low income households. Obligated parties had to achieve 18% of the required energy savings for the 2015 -2017 period (equivalent to 25% on an annual basis for 2016 -2017) through actions in low income households. The sub-target was maintained to 25% of the total obligation for the 2018 -2021 period. These White Certificates are labelled ‘energy poverty’ and are registered (and traded) separately from the ‘classical’ White Certificates. Bonus certificates (uplift factor of 2) were granted for actions for ‘very low income’ households until the end of 2021. These ‘bonus’ certificates were removed from the results reported to the EED energy savings obligation. Since 2022, the scope of the energy poverty sub-target is focused on very low-income households. Therefore, the bonus was removed. The bonus certificates and the combination of EEOS delivery with other national and local funding streams has been effective in ensuring that the energy poverty ringfence target is met and that a significant proportion of savings have been delivered amongst the very low-income group, paving the way to focus on the very low-income group from 2022. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 44 of the White Certificates delivered were ‘energy poverty’ certificates. 74 This high share of ‘energy poverty’ white certificates was achieved also thanks to other bonuses (“coup de pouce”) that promote specific action types (e.g. roof insulation; replacement of fossil fuel boilers with non-fossil fuel heating systems). The “coup de pouce” bonus is higher for actions done in low -income households. These bonuses and uplift factors are also removed when France reports final energy savings to the EED energy savings obligation. Therefore , the share of ‘energy poverty’ savings reported by France to the energy savings obligation is lower. It was , for example, 24.5% for the energy savings reported about 2021 (NECPR data). In addition, the French Ministry in charge of energy (public authority in charge of the scheme) issues calls for specific programmes, including programmes tackling energy poverty. These programmes are accompanying measures (e.g. to identify households at risk of energy poverty and provide them with tailored support). Some of them are the continuation of specific programme s implemented from 2010. These programmes continue to be rewarded based on a fix ed rate of kWh cumac per euro invested. The corresponding White Certificates are not reported to the EED energy savings obligation. However, most of them contribute to triggering further energy efficiency actions eligible to ‘energy poverty’ certificates that are reported to the energy savings obligation. In Ireland, 5% of the energy savings targets in the 2014 -2020 period needed to be delivered in energy poor households. These households are defined as receiving types of welfare transfers or as located in ‘areas designated for revitalisation’. Energy savings in the e nergy poor sector were also supported by grants from government programmes, encouraging synergies between obligated parties and public schemes. The same sub-target continues and is now focused on deeper renovations, i.e. renovation projects reaching minimum thresholds of energy saving gains or high energy performance rating. In the United Kingdom, the Carbon Emissions Reduction Target EEOS (in place between 2008 and 2012) established sub -targets for a 'Priority Group' and, from 2011, a ' Super Priority Group ' of households at risk of energy poverty. Both of these groups were defined in terms of eligibility for certain social benefit payments. In parallel, the UK’s Community Energy Savings Programme (CESP) EEOS (2009-2012) required energy savings to be made in low-income areas (areas that had a high score on the Index of Multiple Deprivation)75. Illustrating the effectiveness of combining EEOS and public schemes to tackle energy poverty, the presence of supporting programme s and funding schemes put in place by the Scottish Government was credited with attracting more measures installed u nder historic UK EEOSs per number of households in Scotland than in many other devolved nations and regions of the UK.76 In Scotland, the framework includes a national, free, independent advice service on energy efficiency and low and zero emission heating, which acts as a referral scheme for further support. Area-based schemes designed and delivered by local authorities, in conjunction with energy companies and local delivery partners leverage EEOS investment and private investment. They focus on reaching those at risk of energy poverty and in ‘harder to treat’ homes including mixed tenure, multiple-occupancy properties and those that require higher -cost insulation measures like solid 74 Ministère de la Transition écologique (2021), Lettre d’information CEE 20210930, https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2021-09%20lettre%20d%27infos%20VF.pdf. 75 https://dclgapps.communities.gov.uk/imd/iod_index.html For a detailed feedback about the experience with CESP, see the final evaluation report: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/350722/CERT_CESP_Evaluation_F INAL_Rep ort.pdf. 76 Ipsos MORI, CAG Consultants and BRE, 2014.
