text: Fraunhofer ISI | 45 wall insulation. In addition to the areabased schemes, Warmer Homes Sc otland is the Scottish Government’s flagship fuel poverty scheme. It complements the UK EEOS by providing subsidies to low-income households, particularly for low and zero emissions heating schemes for communities in rural locations and not served by the gas grid, which are not prioritised by utilities delivering the EEOS. In addition to the explicit fuel poverty schemes and available to the entire population, the Scottish framework also provides zero interest loans, with up to 75% cashback for the cost of measures, and an equity release loan so that asset rich but income poor households can improve the efficiency of their homes.77 The UK’s Energy Company Obligation (ECO) EEOS (2013 -present) contains elements of both of these aspects of policy design (targeting by eligibility for social benefit payments and targeting by geographic area). In its first and second phases, ECO included both a Carbon Saving Community Obligation (an areabased obligation) and a Home Heating Cost Reduction Obligation (HHCRO) (an obligation targeted on delivering energy efficiency measures to low-income households). From 2018, ECO has been fully focused on energy poverty alleviation through an expanded HHCRO, with 15% of the target needing to be delivered in rural areas and 8.7% of th e target needing to be delivered through solid wall-insulation actions. The UK has experimented the LA (Local Authorities) Flex Scheme in its EEOS (ECO: Energy Company Obligation). With the LA Flex scheme, obligated parties are allowed to work with municipalities to better target energy poverty actions and reduce the search costs associated with finding those most in need. The LA Flex Scheme allows local authorities to define their own eligibility criteria, providing them with more ownership and increasing the likelihood of collaboration to address energy poverty issues. In Croatia, the Regulation of the EEOS System (OG 41/2019) states that EEOS should encourage energy efficiency in households affected by energy poverty or social housing 78, and the Croatian EEOS Rulebook states that energy savings in areas with developmental difficulties will receive a 10% uplift, while energy savings in ‘endangered customer’ households will get a 20% uplift. This means that energy savings of 1 ktoe in these categories can be counted as 1. 1 ktoe and 1.2 ktoe respectively. The Croatian EEOS thus allows an ‘area-based’ approach for obligated parties to target their programmes to tackle energy poverty. In Cyprus, the new EEOS planned that actions in energy poor households will receive a bonus factor of 1.5 (i.e. a 50% uplift) on each eligible energy saving. 6.2.2 Alternative measures (Article 10) One major challenge for alternative measures tackling energy poverty is to ensure an effective targeting. The targeting of the policy measures is most often a balance between taking into account the various factors and conditions creating risks of energy p overty and keeping the eligibility/targeting criteria simple to avoid increasing too much the related administration costs and the difficulty for households to apply for support. Among Alternative Measures, various grant schemes include different grant rates according to income levels (e.g. publ ic service obligation on DSOs in Flanders, energy grants for citizen in Wallonia, Clean air programme in Poland). Criteria related to income levels or other social criteria 77 Annex B of https://www.gov.scot/publications/heat -buildings-strategy-achieving-net-zero-emissions-scotlands-buildings/. 78 The regulation of the EEOS (OG 41/2019) states that the scheme should encourage energy efficiency in households affected by energy poverty or in social housing, and include an additional category to recognis e vulnerable customers defined as follows: ‘residential areas of beneficiaries of compensation for vulnerable energy buyers in accordance with the regulation on social welfare and in households in special state welfare areas (i.e. less developed regions), encouraged according to the provisions of the law governing regional development’.

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 46 (such as eligibility to social benefits) are also commonly used to focus a scheme exclusivel y on vulnerable households, often with high incentive rates (up to 100%), acknowledging that the specific target groups do not have financial capacities to carry out energy efficiency actions. For example, the MEBAR II programme79 in Wallonia provides grants to vulnerable households for work to improve the energy efficiency of their dwellings (for owners -occupiers or for tenants). The eligibility criteria are based on thresholds of income levels according to current social policies. The grant can cover 100% of the costs up to a maximum amount. One of the limitations of approaches based on income criteria or eligibility to social benefits is that they do not take into account some of the conditions creating risks of energy poverty, and particularly the level of energy performance of the dwellings. Likewise, an approach based on data from energy bills and bill arrears might not identify households who will restrict their use of energy to avoid bill arrears and disconnection. An alternative way to ensure an effective targeting can be to include targeted energy advice or mini-audits as the first step in the strategies to deliver actions. In Flanders, the DSOs must offer a dedicated information service to the vulnerable households, including free energy scans. From 2005 to 2020, over 200 000 energy scans have been done (up to 20 000/year)80. The energy scan is a 2 to 3-hour visit including a basic energy audit, a comparison of energy suppliers (to switch to a cheaper contract), small energy saving actions (up to 20 Euros) and tips on energy consumption behaviours and further energy saving actions. In the future, the data collected through the energy scans could help to target energy efficiency programmes to help households that are most at risk of energy poverty81. The recent call for co -financing home refurbishments by the Croatian energy efficiency fund specifies that energy auditors can find and engage with vulnerable households to help them apply for the funds. The fund also covers the cost of the energy audit for selected households. Another important point is that households at risk of energy poverty may be very diverse and face different difficulties. Wallonia provides an interesting example of complementary schemes that are designed to take into account that households at risk of energy poverty can face very different situations and need different forms of support. The four schemes described briefly below have been reported to the EED energy savings obligation. First, the main grant schemes for energy renovation (“Primes Habitation” 82 / Housing Grants) provide grants with amounts depending on the income level, with a factor from 1 (highest incomes eligible) to 6 (lowest income category). This acknowledges that the financial capacity of the households is most often correlated to their income. Second, the Rénopack scheme 83 provides a 0% -interest loan to finance the remaining costs of renovation or energy-saving works in dwellings, as a complement to the Housing Grant. This loan scheme is mana ged by two social credit institutions, ensuring access to credit for low -income households. It acknowledges that low -income households would otherwise have difficulties to cover the remaining costs (despite the higher Housing Grant they get), and to access credit. 79 https://energie.wallonie.be/fr/obtenir-une-aide-en-tant-que-menage-a-bas-revenus.html?IDC=6369 80 It was estimated that in Flanders about 260 000 households have energy expenses higher than 10% of their income. 81 https://www.ca-eed.eu/content/download/8276/file/WG4.2%20Energy%20poverty%20Flemish%20Energy%20Agency.pdf/attachment 82 https://energie.wallonie.be/fr/primes-habitation-a-partir-du-1er-juin-2019.html?IDC=9792 83 https://www.wallonie.be/fr/demarches/beneficier-du-renopack

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 47 Third, for households who cannot enter into deep renovation s or costly actions, the MEBAR II scheme84 provides a 100% grant of up to 1 365 euros per household to help with ' intermediate cost' works. It is restricted to low-income households (social integration income plus 20%, i.e. about EUR 1 597 per month for a household), owner-occupiers or tenants, for energy saving works (e.g., insulation, heating system, replacement of windows or external doors). The same household can get this grant again after a period of 5 years: this condition ensures that 1) the same households do not get the grant every year (to reach more households over time), but 2) there is still the possibility for households to make successive improvements, when it is difficult for them to carry out larger works at once. Fourth, for the most vulnerable households, the PAPE scheme85 provides regional aids to the CPAS (municipal social services) to initiate Preventive Energy Action Plans (PAPE). This includes tailored support to households in precarious situations, whether or not they are beneficiaries of the CPAS: energy assessment, advice and information, support for low -cost actions, home visits, etc. The scheme also includes information and sessions raising awareness about how to save energy, how to access available aids and grants, etc. The support provided is equivalent to EUR 200 per household. This amount is advanced by the CPAS, then reimbursed to the households according to their income and the achieved energy savings. About addressing the upfront investment cost in condominiums, in the Czech Republit, part of the Green Savings programme86 supporting energy renovation of apartment buildings includes also vulnerable consumers. If the housing cooperative or homeowner association applies for the programme, the individual households do not need to spend any additional money. The cost of renovation is funded by loans or savings of the housing cooperatives or home-owner associations. They receive the subsidy after the renovation. Several Member States have implemented schemes to provide low-income or vulnerable households with energy advice, and, when relevant, financial support to replace inefficient appliances. Since 2008, Caritas Germany is offering the ‘Stromspar-Check’, energy saving advice for low-income households that was disseminated in more than 150 municipalities. Long-term unemployed people are trained to advice households with low income on how to lower their energy costs. The project offers non-obligatory advice for people who otherwise have little to do with issues like energy saving and environmental protection. Each consultation is individually tailored to the customer‘s consumption of e lectricity, water and heating. Each participating household receives a complete measuring of all energy and water consuming devices as well as a detailed report, as well as hardware (energy saving bulbs, water -saving shower heads, etc.) according to the results of the individual report and worth up to EUR 70. The participants can also receive a voucher (EUR 100 to EUR 200) to replace their inefficient cooling appliance (if older than 10 years) with a high efficiency one. Long-term unemployed people are qualified to become energyand water-saving consultants, going through a specially designed training programme. More than 1 200 were trained since 2008, and more than 800 are currently working. Caritas has been offering a similar scheme in Austria (‘Stromhilfefonds’) since 201088. As a part of th e Malta’s energy efficiency plan for 2020, its Energy and Water agency conducted about 500 visits to socially vulnerable households. In addition to sharing useful tips on how to save energy and water on a daily basis, the visits included an assessment of the appliances being used. Out of the 470 visits conducted, 277 households were identified as needing an appliance replacement. The range of appliances to be replaced was restricted to fridge -freezers, washing machines and air conditioning (AC) units , as th ese are considered to have the highest energy consumption. In total, 189 fridge -freezers, 40 washing machines and 23 AC units were replaced. Old units were collected and disposed of. A follow up phase has been scheduled. The cabinet of Cyprus approved a EUR 5 million scheme in late 2021 to subsidise the replacement of energy consuming home appliances amongst vulnerable groups. The scheme also includes cutting VAT on bills to 5 % for vulnerable households for six months and to 9 per cent for three months for other consumers. It is estimated that the replacement of old home appliances with newer, energy saving ones, will contribute to over 50% in savings in their energy consumption. The appliances included in the scheme are refrigerators, washing machines and air conditioning units. Eligible consumers can replace up to five appliances, i.e. up to three A/Cs, one washing machine, and one refrigerator. The scheme, published in December 2021, will remain in effect until December 2022 or until the available budget is used up. It is expected that it will cover around 5 000 applications. Grants will range between EUR 300 and EUR 600 depending on the appliance. The request must be submitted by the vulnerable consumers themselves and the old appliances to be replaced will be collected by the supplier for recycling purposes and a certificate must be obtained. The pro-visions include minimum energy efficiency classes for new models (A++ or higher for cooling and A+ or higher for heating for air -conditioners; C or higher for washing machines; D or higher for refrigerators). 6.3 Policy measures for building renovation The energy renovation of buildings is a major part of the energy efficiency strategy in most Member States. It has also been flagged as one of the priorities of the EU Green Deal, through the Renovation Wave initiative. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 49 among the main public schemes implemented by Member States to promote energy renovation93. In parallel, many projects have been funded by the EU to develop innovative approaches for energy renovation94 or to identify the needs in capacity building and skil ls among building professionals through the Build Up Skills initiative 95. A joint initiative of the European Commi ssion and the construction industry, EeB PPP (Energy efficient Buildings Public Private Partnership), is also supporting the development of breakthrough affordable technical and business-driven solutions at building and district scale, from early stage conception to demonstration of almost ready-to-market innovations. Parts of the projects initiated with EeB PPP are related to renovation of buildings96. 6.3.1 EEOS (Article 9) The first distinction to be observed concerns whether or not the EEOS allows the combination of obligated parties’ technical and financial support with public incentives. When this combination is not allowed, the share of energy savings achieved by obligated parties in buildings, and especially in the residential sector, is usually limited. EEOSs are ind eed meant to promote the most costeffective actions. Obligated parties can often find more cost-effective options with energy efficiency projects in industry that may require smaller incentives to be triggered. Moreover, projects in industry can be significantly larger than projects in buildings, thereby reducing the transaction costs for a same amount of energy savings. At the opposite, EEOSs allowing the combination of obligated parties’ incentives with public incentives have been successful in achieving a large amount of energy savings in buildings, including in the residential sector, as in France for example. Another example is Ireland, where this combination is allowed and obligated parties shall achieve a minimum share (20%) of energy savings in the residential sector, a residential ringfence (in addition to the 5% for the energy poverty ringfence mentioned above). Moreover, the redesign of the Irish EEOS for its new period plans to require projects reported to the residential ringfence to deliver measures that result in achievement of a minimum level of energy savings, a minimum energy performance after the works (Bu ilding Energy Rating B297 or < 125 kWh /m² per year) or set the home onto a pathway to achieve B2 with an advisory report showing the complete path (similar approach as building renovation passport). Experience has indeed shown that, when delivering energy savings in buildings, EEOSs tend to mostly deliver single energy efficiency actions or shallow renovations. Hence the new provisions in the Iri sh scheme and also a special bonus to promote deep renovations in the French white certificates scheme. As these provisions are recent, it is yet too early to know their actual impacts. 93 https://ec.europa.eu/jrc/en/publication/eur-scientific-and-technical-research-reports/accelerating-energy-renovation-investments-buildings. 94 See for example, the report prepared by EAMSE summarizing seven recent project working with public and private actors to achi eve higher renovation rates with higher energy efficiency levels (EmBuild, HERON, NewTREND, REFURB, RentalCal, TRANSITION ZERO (d isseminating the Energiesprong approach) and URBAN LEARNING): https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/7726dd32-f6b1-11e8-9982-01aa75ed71a1/language-en/format-PDF/ About older projects (funded through the Intelligent Energy Europe programme), see for example the evaluation done in 2017: https://ec.europa.eu/easme/sites/easme-site/files/stc-evaluation_of_iee_buildings_projects_under_iee_ii_main_report_23_november_clean.pdf . 95 About recent results, see for example: https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/73fde71a-25fb-11ea-af81-01aa75ed71a1/language-en/format-PDF. 96 See the 2019 project review: http://www.ectp.org/fileadmin/user_upload/documents/E2B/0_EeB_PPP_Project -Reviews_Roadmaps/EeB_PPP_Project_Review_2019.pdf. 97 The Building Energy Rating is Ireland’s Energy Performance Certificate.

BEG ). • Including ex post on -site inspections of the works (e.g. Croatian programme for energy renovation of multifamily buildings). • Possibility to combine financial aids from obligated parties and from public programme s to stimulate a larger number of actions and to provide high grant rates to low income or vulnerable households (e.g. in France and Ireland). • Involvement of local authorities to improve the targeting of the most inefficient buildings and/or households the most in need (e.g. Ireland and the United Kingdom). • Law facilitating the decision to make renovation works in co -owned buildings, and possibility to pass progressively the costs to tenants through increases in maintenance charges over a number of years (e.g. Lithuania). • Favouring the set-up of housing associations to own and manage apartment blocks, creating easier conditions for renovation plans supported with grants, soft loans and information (Slovakia). • National funds whose one of the missions or objectives is to provide financial aids for building renovations (e.g. national energy efficiency funds in Croatia and Spain, Eko Sklad/EcoFund in Slovenia). • Use of revenues from carbon credits as one of the funding sources for renovation programmes (e.g. Green Savings programme in Czech Republic, SlovSEFF III in Slovakia, ‘Habiter Mieux’ (Living Better) programme taking part in the white certificates scheme in France). • Qualification scheme and label for building professionals as part of the criteria for actions to be eligible to white certificates (e.g. France). This list of examples does not aim to be exhaustive: other countries might implement the same practices or provisions as described above, and other types of interesting practices or examples can surely be found among the large numbers of policy measures pr omoting building renovations in the set of policy measures reported to the energy savings obligation during 2014 -2020 and now for 2021-2030. This selection is based on elements that could be clearly identified in the reporting from Member States to the Eur opean Commission, and , whenever possible , that were also confirmed as interesting examples from other sources. Further examples and good practices can be found for example in the "Report on renovation of the national stock of residential and non -residential buildings and on nearly zero -energy buildings under regulation (EU) 2018/1999 as part of the 8 th State of the Energy Union 99, or in the documentation related to the Renovation Wave initiative100. 98 Some have interactions with EEOS, as noted in the list. 99 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/publications/report-renovation-national-stock-residential-and-non-residential-buildings_en. 100 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-buildings/renovation-wave_en

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 51 6.4 Policy measures for transport and mobility The policy measures specifically focused on transport represented only 5% of the cumulative savings achieved over 2014–2020. This share is likely higher in practice, as some cross-cutting policy measures include energy savings from transport, particularly some EEOS (e.g. Austria, France, Greece and Slovenia) and taxation measures (e.g. Cyprus and Greece). Nevertheless, the share of energy savings reported from transport has remained small compared to the share of transport in the final energy consumption and the related energy savings potential. At the same time, policy measures can be major components of the strategy in some Member States. Moreover, when Member States have not reported policy measures in transport to the energy savings obligation, it does not mean that they do not implement energy efficiency policies in transport. The reason why they do not report these policies can be due to higher difficulties to monitor energy savings from transport, because of potential risks of overlaps with cross -cutting measures (and that these overlaps would be difficult to quantify), because they want to give priority to measures in other sectors or because policies for transport are managed separately from the other energy efficiency policies. 6.4.1 Energy efficiency obligation scheme (Article 9) In the period 2014-2020, 9 EEOS have allowed obligated parties to report energy savings achieved in transport: Austria, Bulgaria, Croatia, France, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg and Slovenia. However, only three of these EEOS have seen a significant share (higher than 5%) of energy savings in transport: Austria, Greece and Slovenia. This was partly due to the eligibility of fuel additives monitored with deemed savings that have been revised since then. France’s white certificates scheme is likely the scheme where most calculation methods have been prepared to support the implementation and reporting of actions in transport: the catalogue of standardised actions includes 36 types of eligible actions in transport101. Moreover, from January 2023, two bonuses are promoting car-pooling for short 102 and long 103 distance, respectively. Obligated parties can also achieve part of their target by funding accompanying programmes, with some of them being focused on mobility. Between January 2022 and September 2023, white certificates from actions in transport amounted to 2.5% (31.6 TWh cumac 104) of the total white certificates issued. 6.4.2 Alternative measures (Article 10) As reminded in Appendix VII of the 2019 EC Recommendation on transposing the energy savings obligations under the EED, policies to achieve energy savings in transport can be categorised according to three main axes of action: • reducing the need to travel, • shifting travel to more energy-efficient modes and/or • improving the efficiency of transport modes. 101 See (in French): https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/operations-standardisees-deconomies-denergie#scroll-nav__9. 102 See more details (in French): https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/coup -pouce-covoiturage-courte-distance. 103 See more details (in French): https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/coup -pouce-covoiturage-longue-distance. 104 TWh cumac is the unit for white certificates, in terms lifetime -cumulated and discounted energy savings.

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 52 More details about possible types of policy measures for each axis can be found in this Appendix. Concrete examples are mentioned below, grouping them according to the three axes listed above. None of the policy measures reported so far to the energy savings obligation include explicitly the objective to reduce the demand for travel. This can, however, be affected by taxation measures, such as taxes on fuel for transport (as reported for example by Czech Republic, Finland and Lithuania, or as part of cross -cutting taxes that cover transport in Cyprus and Greece). Three countries have reported travel taxes, either km-tax or tolls for trucks (Austria, Belgium and Germany) or air passenger duty (Germany). These travel taxes can have effects in terms of modal shift (e.g. to rail mode) or in reducing travel demand and improving the energy efficiency per goods carried (by providing an incentive to freight companies to optimi se the truck loads). As the reporting to the energy savings obligation is focused on energy savings, it has not yet included documentation about possible effects in terms of reducing the demand for travel or modal shift. Umbrella policies or strategies for transport or mobility (as reported by Austria, Hungary, Romania, Slovakia and Spain) usually include elements to promote modal shift. More specific measures focused on public transport infrastructures are clearly aiming at modal shift (e.g. metro extensions reported by Greece, Hungary and Romania). Other examples of measures promoting modal shift include companies’ mobility plans (as reported by the Brussels region), city bike systems (as reported by Croatia), and subsidies to decrease cost of public transport (as reported by Hungary or Portugal). In practice, most of the transport measures reported to the energy savings obligation in 2014-2020 aim at improving the efficiency of transport modes, and particularly road vehicles. The predominance of measures related to improving the efficiency of transport modes might be because energy savings from these measures are easier to monitor, and their energy savings effects are easier to demonstrate. The reported transport policy measures target private passenger travel, public transport and freight. A few measures had a specific scope: a fleet management system for the Central government’s vehicles (Cyprus), the PIMA Tierra scheme for tractors (Spain), waterway and air transport modernisation (Romania). Italy has reported to the EED energy savings obligation its Ferrobonus and Marebonus programmes promoting modal shift for freight , shift to rail and sea transport respectively 105. Energy savings from both programmes represent 29% of the new annual energy savings reported by Italy for 2021. Concerning the improvement of vehicle energy efficiency, it must be observed that that only energy savings for early replacements of vehicles are eligible. Otherwise, energy savings from new vehicles are not counted as additional compared to the EU emission standards for vehicles (see the Annex to the 2019 Recommendation106 for more details). The ‘early replacement’ condition can be met by targeting car scrappage or retrofit schemes targeted at the oldest or most -inefficient cars, possibly with income -related conditions. To make it affordable for low -income households, one option is to allow the replacement of the old car with a second-hand car meeting minimum energy performance criteria (or having an emission level below a given threshold). This can provide incentives for the purchase of secondhand cars bringing already a significant gain compared to very old and inefficient cars, as done in France107. 105 For more details about these programmes and the calculation methodologies, see the presentation made at the streamSAVE workshop on modal shift for freight: https://streamsave.flexx.camp/support -contribution-821. 106 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reco/2019/1658/oj. 107 A scrappage scheme focused on low-income households and allowing the replacement with second -hand cars has been implemented in France for several years (details in French): https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/prime -conversion-bonus-ecologique-toutes-aides-en-faveur-

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 53 An alternative can be retrofit schemes where the internal combustion engine is replaced with an electric motor, which can be less expensive than buying a new electric vehicle. 6.5 Taxation measures (Article 10(4)) Several Member States have reported taxation measures in 2014–2020, including measures in the form of excise duties on electricity, natural gas and oil products (for transport and space heating), or on specific energy products. An essential point is that, in order for taxation to generate real energy saving impacts, it should aim f or structural effects and facilitate the energy market transformation. The taxation measures reported by Sweden are a good example, where, first, the tax rate is high enough to provide a clear price signal, and second, taxation measures are part of a comprehensive strategy for energy and climate. It has been thought of as a cornerstone policy since the 1990s, thus generating the desired energy savings and increasing the market responsiveness of the consumers. Taxation is also an important measure that can be used in parallel and complementing other alternative measures, enhancing their effectiveness. More specifically, the signal on the price increase of energy sources can further stimulate the adoption and pur chase of energy efficiency measures and products, when especially the latter are being supported by subsidy measures in the households and SME sectors. This effect is reinforcing and can help to further accelerate energy savings in the overall policy mix. To demonstrate energy savings from taxation measures, it is equally important to carry out an analysis for the counterfactual energy consumption , which must be compared with the resulting observed energy consumption and disentangle the effect of the measure. This analysis must be documented with solid scientific values for short and medium/long run elasticities, as was the case in several Member St ates (such as Cyprus and Sweden as reported in the NECP). Related useful resources on methodologies and values for elasticities can be found in Csereklyei (2020)108, Bianco et al., (2020)109, Labandeira et al., (2016)110, Europe Economics (2016)111 and other related studies with econometric modelling. As these studies may provide now outdated values (for benchmarking), it is highly recommended to carry out new national studies and regularly review the most recent publications in the field. 6.6 Eligibility of e nergy saving s under the European Emission Trading System (EU-ETS 1 and 2) Under Article 10a of the ETS Directive112, if an installation is covered by the obligation to conduct an energy audit or to implement a certified energy management system under the EED, the amount of free allocation of ETS allowances will be reduced by 20%, unless the recommendations of the audit (or certified energy management system (CEMS)) with pay-backs of three years or less have lacquisition-vehicules-propres#scroll-nav__2. It has been evaluated in 2021 (evaluation report in French): https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/thema_essentiel_12_prime_a_la_conversion_des_vehicules_octobre2021.pdf It was successful in the number of replacements and efficiency gains, but with some drawbacks in dealing with the replaced cars as recycling capacities were not enough. 108 https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301421519306664 109 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7178152/ 110 https://cadmus.eui.eu/handle/1814/40870 111 https://ec.europa.eu/energy/sites/ener/files/documents/final_report_on_fiscal_measures_used_under_article_7_eed_0.pdf 112 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02003L0087-20230605

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 54 been implemented, the costs of the investments are disproportionate or other measures have been implemented which lead to greenhouse gas emission reductions equivalent to the energy efficiency improvement recommendations. Energy savings from energy efficiency actions required to receive the free allocation of ETS allowances are ineligible to be accounted under the energy savings obligations. Article 22a of the update of the Free Allocation Rules113 provides more details on the definition of disproportionate investment costs as well as clarifying that recommendations leading to energy savings outside the system boundaries of the industrial process carried out at the installation (and therefore not covered by the EU -ETS) do not affect the free allocation of allowances. This means that energy savings from recommendations in office buil dings on an industrial site, for example, would remain eligible under the energy savings obligations.114 Some policy measures deliver final energy savings in ETS industrial installations receiving free allocation. Examples include most white certificates schemes or EEOS , voluntary agreements in Belgium (Flanders and Wallonia) , Bulgaria’s Operational programme ‘Innovation and Competitiveness’ for increasing energy efficiency in large enterprises, Romania’s programme for energy efficiency in ETS industries, and formerly the Netherlands’ long-term agreement for energyintensive industries (MEE). In these cases, the policy measure may need to be adjusted to ensure that all energy savings are eligible or ex post adjustments made to energy savings to remove ineligible energy savings. Policy me asures can automatically adjust to ensure that energy savings are eligible by using payback criteria. An example of this was Denmark’s energy efficiency auction programme that only supported energy efficiency projects above payback threshold. Similarly, France’s white certificates scheme allows energy savings in ETS sites since the law n° 2019-486 (May 2019), and more specifically the by -law published in September 2019 (Decree n°2019975). This decree set the requirements and eligibility conditions. In addition to requiring measurements for at least 6 months (or 2 months in the case of small projects), the decree requires that the value of the ETS credits is taken into account when calculating the payback time against the eligibility criteria. This value is set by decree for every year (e.g. EUR 9.54 /tCO2e for 2019, EUR 22.41 /tCO2e for 2020). The current EU -ETS (ETS 1) covers large industrial installations, the power sector, aviation and shipping. The extension of emissions trading beyond electricity to other fuels used in buildings, road transport and the rest of the industrial sector (ETS 2) means that virtually all energy end-uses are covered by the ETS. Energy savings from eligible energy efficiency policy measures in the sectors covered by both ETS 1 and ETS 2 continue to count towards Member States’ obligations if they comply with the measurement, verification and energy savings calculation requirements of Annex V. Policy makers can adapt their existing programme s as a result of changes to the ETS Directive. Increases in the cost of fossil fuels will mean that some energy efficiency actions may no longer require policy support and others may require less support (e.g. lower subsidies) or that higher energy savings can be achieved with the same support. 6.7 Monitoring & Verification practices M&V systems are a crucial component of effective implementation and accurate reporting of energy efficiency policies. It is often challenging to balance between accuracy and high costs when specifying the requirements of a successful M&V system. One effective way to both monitor and verify energy savings is through IT systems. Another is through straightforward reporting 113 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2024/873/oj 114 https://climate.ec.europa.eu/document/download/6bdefaa1-2aa8-4306-a4a2-4eb7d751f5ae_en?filename=12_gd12_eneff_conditionality_en.pdf

An additional important issue for successful M&V is controlling the quality of actions installed, especially by ensuring that a statistically significant proportion of measures is verified. This section gathers some interesting examples and useful resources on how certain Member States tackle these issues. Several Member States use IT systems to collect and process data, either for all measures or for some sectors, while others use written protocols and either systematic or random checks . A prerequisite for having an accurate and transparent M&V system in place is prescribing common measurement methods. The Horizon 2020 project multEE (2015–2017) developed resources for developing Monitoring & Verification systems, including the review of current practices and recommendations for enhanced practices. The Horizon 2020 project ENSMOV (2019 -2022), followed by the LIFE project ENSMOV Plus (2022-2025), have both prepared summaries about good practices for cost -effective M&V, gathering examples from various countries. The Horizon 2020 project streamSAVE (2020-2023) has developed a set of calculation methodologies for 10 Priori ty Actions , tested and discussed in partner countries, and complemented with dialogue meetings that gathered further good practices on calculation methods. The final event of streamSAVE, jointly organised with the DEESME project (energy efficiency for SME) in June 2023, largely focused on the development of M&V practices115. Similarly, ENSMOV Plus organised two online workshops on M&V in July and September 2023 about setting up an M&V system and using measurements respectively 116. As a complement to M&V practices, the Horizon 2020 proje ct EPATEE (2017-2019) developed resources for enhanced policy evaluations, including case studies, a knowledge base on evaluations and an evaluation toolbox. See Table 2 in section 6.8 below about links and short descriptions of these projects. 6.7.1 Energy efficiency obligation scheme (Article 9) Implementing EEOS implies a strong M&V system to allow obligated parties, and possibly other stakeholders (especially in white certificates schemes), to report energy efficiency actions or projects to get them validated and credited for the achievement of their individual target. General guidelines for M&V systems for EEOS can be found in the review of market -based instruments done by the IEA in 2017 117. For most EEOS, the M&V rules of the scheme have been aligned with the requirements set in Annex V EED, especially to comply with the provisions on materiality, additionality and avoiding double counting. Common rules about materiality are for obligated parties to have evidence of the support provided and that it was offered before the action was decided. Additionality is usually addressed in the eligibility criteria for the energy efficiency actions or projects and in the rules to set the baseline to calculate energy savings. Double counting is tracked by requiring obligated parties to report identifiers for all beneficiaries (e.g. postal address, number of electricity meter) . Typical evidence about materiality and double counting is a declaration on honour signed b y the beneficiary. This provides a legal basis to engage responsibilities of the beneficiary and obligated party (or its contractor) in the case of controls. For most EEOS , obligated parties are required to store , for a given period , all administrative documents (e.g. invoices, declaration of honours) that could be needed in the case of a control. Usually, only part of the documentation needs to be submitted when applying for validation of the energy savings. Moreover, most EEOS have developed online platforms, or templates of 115 See: https://streamsave.eu/finalevent/ 116 See: https://energysavingpolicies.eu/policy-cycle/monitoring-reporting-and-verification/ 117 https://www.iea.org/reports/market-based-instruments-for-energy-efficiency

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 56 electronic files, to facilitate the submission of applications by the obligated parties or other stakeholders and then to automatize part of the checks and validation of the applications. This also makes sampling easier to combine targeted and random controls. Another important component of the M&V system is to allow beneficiaries , consumer organisations and other relevant entities in the national context, to report problems and frauds. This can be managed by existing administrations in charge of consumer protection and fraud prevention or by appointing an ombudsman dedicated to the EEOS. The first option is chosen more frequently and requires coordination between different administrations (e.g. authority in charge of the EEOS and administration in charge of consumer protection), to share and cross data. This may also imply coordination with the fiscal administration to prevent companies already detected as fraudulent from having projects validated in the EEOS. Looking at national examples, Ireland has set an online energy savings crediting system for actions in the residential sector. Obligated parties must implement an ISO 9001 -aligned quality control process using ISO 50015 or IPVMP for M&V in the non-residential sectors. This ensures that the companies doing work for obligated parties have quality assurance regimes in place and that the workers are appropriately accredited. The reassurance that this requirement brings enables the implementing body (SEAI) to target its independent audits on specific areas. A key parameter for the success of EEOS is to find a good balance between the reliability of reported energy savings (including controls when needed) and low administration costs for obligated parties. The latter is essential to make it attractive for obligated parties to meet their target with energy efficiency programmes instead of paying a penalty or contributing to an energy efficiency fund. The United Kingdom, for example, introduced an M&V system in 2013, which calculated the energy savings for their Energy Company Obligation (ECO) focused on the residential sector, using the Standard Assessment Procedure (SAP)118, instead of energy savings being previously credi ted with deemed scores for insulation and heating system replacements. Using SAP, even in a simplified way for the ECO, required the input of many data that affect energy performance. In 2018, the ECO moved to scaled savings for these types of actions to reduce administration costs and free up funds for investment in energy efficiency technologies. The example of Denmark's EEOS shows the difficulty to balance monitoring and verification on the one hand and the associated cost and administrative burden on the other hand. The EEOS in Denmark were successful in the industry sector, with a positive social -economic evaluation, b ut were stopped by the end of 2020. In Denmark, the target was raised several times, and the obligated parties were overachieving. As a result of the increased obligation from 2010 onwards in the Danish scheme, significantly more energy savings have been realised in industry , as found in other EEOS where combining incentives from obligated parties and public incentives are not allowed in the residential sector. However, there is some concern that some of the energy savings were free-riders (measures which would have been introduced anyway) in the industry sector, but probably even more in households. The Danish EEOS wa s characterized by fewer controls compared to other European EEOSs and was guided by flexibility and trust in the correct reporting by the companies. Controls were performed by sample. The energy efficiency saving goals have been increased annually (the energy savings target was almost doubled each year). This put the obligated companies under a lot of pressure, which might have led to the overestimation of energy savings. This could be overcome with stricter monitoring and more controls. But too strict definitions, overcontrolling and high administrative burden were perceived as ending the possibility of cost - 118 Equivalent to an Energy Performance Certificate for buildings. In practice, what was required was a simplified form of SAP.

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 57 effective energy savings. Danish EEOS had an objective to realise the set target at minimum costs, regardless of sector and energy form. Concerning the control and quality of the energy efficiency actions installed, having an IT tool in place is just one efficient, but administratively challenging, example. Another less costly example is setting practices and rules to be followed by all parties involved. For example, Ireland introduced the Assigned Certifier role in 2014 for each building project covered by building codes. The Assigned Certifier is responsible for declaring that the energy related elements ( among others) of the project comply with the building codes, and they must be a registered professional (Chartered Engineer, Chartered Building Surveyor or Registered Architect) with relevant experience and competency in relation to complex construction projects. In the end, all energy savings, whether collected one by one, or aggregated through an IT system, should be verified. Achieving this balance between the accuracy of calculated energy savings and the costs/time involved in reporting is never straightforward. An important example demonstrating the need for right balance between accuracy and the easiness of reporting energy savings is Italy’s White Certificates scheme: after issues with fraud, an IT system strengthened the M&V regime. However, this resulted in some difficulties in the market, and many project applications were rejected. The current production of white certificates remains lower than the expectations119. France’s white certificates scheme also needed to mitigate an increase in fraud related to the increase in the energy savings targets and the turnovers that achieving these energy savings targets imply (similar to the Danish and Italian cases). This was addressed by strengthening auditing and controls by both the public authority in charge of M&V (PNCEE) and the obligated parties or other parties allowed to submit application files (eligible parties). These new provisions on controls were enforced by law n° 20191147 (adopted in N ovember 2019), and further specified in a series of bylaws. Administrative sanctions have been increased, as well as the time limit for PNCEE to make verifications and controls (from 3 to 6 years). Before submitting an application file including standardised actions, obligated or eligible parties shall contract accredited controlling companies to perform on-site checks for at least 10% of the reported actions and remote checks for at least 20% of the reported actions. PNCEE then performs or commissions controls w hen processing applications, combining controls on cases reported by beneficiaries , other administrations or other sources, and random controls. When the controls detect non-compliance or fraud, the corresponding amounts of white certificates are withdrawn and administrative sanctions may apply. In the case of severe fraud, cases may be transferred to the Court. In a few cases raising concerns about embezzlement of funds to foreign countries, TRACFIN, the ministry of economy’s unit in charge of international underground financial circuits and money laundering, also intervened. PNCEE published a synthesis on the controls carried out in 2022120: 6 400 on-site checks (1% of certificates issued in 2022 from standardised actions), 120XXX 000 checks by direct mail (4.2%) and 620 desk checks (0.7%). These checks verify compliance with technical requirements set in the specifications of the standardised actions , th at the reported actions have actually been implemented and comply with the parameters used to calculate energy savings. In 2022, the se checks were supplemented by checks on more than 1 XXX 200 operations, representing almost 6.3 119 For more details, see for example: https://energysavingpolicies.eu/wp -content/uploads/2023/07/Di-Santo-Italian-WhC-scheme.pdf. 120 In French: https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/Contr%C3%B4le%20du%20dispositif%20des%20CEE%20 -%20Bilan%202022_VF.pdf A synthesis of the controls done in the period 2018-2021 can be found in the final report about this period (also in French): https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/2022-02-17-CEE-Bilan-Synthese.pdf.

Moreover, the French white certificates scheme encourages the use of Energy Performance Contracting with guaranteed energy savings : standardised energy saving actions done in residential or tertiary buildings under an Energy Performance Contract get a bonus in terms of white certificates121. The bonus is an uplift factor that depends on the duration of the contract, and the rate of final energy savings guaranteed in the contract (E in the formula below): • For contracts shorter than 10 years: uplift factor = [ 1 + (2 x E) ] • For contracts equal to or longer than 10 years: uplift factor = [ 1 + (3 x E) ] Moreover, the objective of the Energy Performance Contract shall be to achieve energy savings of at least 20% compared to the baseline energy consumption in the scope of the contract. So , for example, a contract with an energy savings target of 25% and lasting 8 years (i.e. less than 10 years) will get an uplift factor of [1 + (2*0.25)] = 1.5. This means that for the standardised actions reported under this contract, these actions will get 50% more white certificates than without the use of an Energy Performance Contract. These ‘bonus’ white certificates are not reported to Article 8 EED, but they provide an incentive to implement Energy Performance Contract. In addition to the ‘bonus’ white certificates, the building owners also be guaranteed through the contract that the actions implemented will achieve at least the rate of energy savings agreed in the contract. The use of Energy Performance Contract is also promoted as a standardised action itself that is credited a standardised amount of certificates per dwelling (for multifamily buildings) or per m² (for tertiary buildings). This amount varies according to the climate zone and the duration of the guarantee on energy savings. Both approaches are specified in a way to avoid overlap and double counting: • The “bonus” approach is focused on the implementation of actions included in the catalogue of standardised actions, such as insulation of the building envelope or replacement of heating system. • The Energy Performance Contract as an action itself is focused on energy savings from improved maintenance, operation and optimisation of energy systems of multifamily or tertiary buildings122. It should be noted that in both cases, the delivered amount of white certificates remains based on deemed savings (it is not calculated from the metered data). However, due to the contr act, the energy savings are monitored with metered data, so that the building owners (or tenants) get a guarantee on the energy savings achieved. Since the white certificates scheme makes use of deemed savings to keep the reporting of these actions simple and to enable delivering the white certificates at once, there is no need to wait for the end of the contract to get the white certificates, which could otherwise create a problem in case of long-term contracts. 6.7.2 Alternative measures (Article 10) Some Member States, like Austria and Croatia use an IT system developed for the measurement and verification of all policy measures they report to the EED energy savings obligation, including 121 See Article 6 of the Order of 29 December 2014 on the terms and conditions of implementation the white certificate scheme: https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/article_lc/LEGIARTI000044956890. 122 Standardised action for multifamily buildings is BAR-SE-105: https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/BAR-SE-105.pdf Standardised action for tertiary buildings is BAT-SE-104: https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/BAT-SE-104.pdf.

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 59 alternative measures and an EEOS (until 2020 for Austria123). The monitoring and verification system in Austria stands out with its quality, precision and transparency, and the Croatian system SMiV124 was made based on the Austrian one. These centralised M&V systems allow to directly track and correct for double counting. It also ensures that harmonised calculation methods are used across all policy measures, creating consistency in the energy savings data. In both countries, the M&V system is operated by a dedicated body (monitoring body in Austria; national coordination body for energy efficiency in Croatia). Such centralised M&V systems require an investment cost, constant management, and regular updates. It has proven to be effective to get regular updates about policy measures’ achievements and progress towards targets. They provide useful information for steering the policy measures and a rapid feedback loop to detect needs for adjustments in M&V rules and other design features of the policy measures. Centralised systems also help optimizing controls when needed. Therefore, these centralised M&V systems come at a significant cost, but also deliver high benefits for policy making and effectiveness . To optimise the running costs of the IT systems , Austria and Croatia have introduced changes to automatise more of the IT process , while maintaining the high-quality assurance. Other Member States use an IT system only for certain measures. Finland, for example, has introduced an online system used in the context of voluntary agreement which helps to streamline reporting125. Some countries, instead, do not use an IT system at all, but invest heavily in the M&V process and controls. The Netherlands is one such example, where the long -term agreements 126 has a demonstrated and long-lasting history of intensive monitoring and verification of energy efficiency. Belgium (Flanders) also has a well-established M&V ensured along the entire process of the voluntary agreements: energy audit plans are submitted by the participating companies and approved by the Verification Office; the energy plans resulting from the energy audits then need to be approved by the Verification Office that can make recommendations and require adjustments to the energy plans submitted by the participating companies (this step includes a review of the energy audits done by the participating companies); the participating companies need to submit a report to the Verification Office each year, including information and data on energy consumption and the progress with implementing the actions included in their energy plan and; in addition to the review of the annual reports, the Verification Office performs on-site inspections. An important point is that participating companies report directly to the Verification Office (no intermediate aggregation by the sectoral federations), which ensures that the Verification Office receives all the data needed to review what each participating company is doing and to organise on -site inspections. This also means that the Verification Office, established as an independent body, ensures data security and confidentiality. The inf ormation published about the scheme only includes aggregated data to ensure data confidentiality, which is a particularly important condition for companies to be willing to join the voluntary agreements. 123 Austria’s EEOS was discontinued at the end of 2020. Therefore, from 2021 on, Austria is reporting alternative measures only. 124 Presentation about SMiV at the CA EED (March 2017). 125 EPATEE case study (2017): Finland: Energy Efficiency Agreement for Industries. https://epatee.eu/system/tdf/epatee_case_study_finland_energy_efficiency_agreement_for_industries_ok_0.pdf?file=1&type=node&i d=68. 126 These long-term agreements were terminated in December 2020, and replaced with an energy savings obligation for companies. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 74 • "In a first step, the data on companies of the public commercial register are used and filtered according to the non-SME definition of the EU (companies are pre-listed). • In a second step, the information on the pre-listed companies are checked (using e.g. financial reports of the companies). If there are no data on the turnover or annual balance sheet of all enterprises in the commercial register, enterprises with more than 250 employees are also listed separately. Similarly, enterprises with no information on the number of employees but whose turnover or annual balance sheet is exceeding the thresholds are listed separately. Information on companies on the list of large enterprises for which there is no information on the number of employees is collected from other sources. • From the data published in the commercial register on the economic indicators of an undertaking, the turnover of the undertaking is considered to be its sales revenue and the total volume of the annual balance sheet is the value of the undertaking's assets. • Companies that are in liquidation or deleted from the commercial register have been removed from the list. • At the end of the process, the list of "obligated companies" is published. Also, the companies are then individually informed by the authorities. • If a company considers that it has fallen below the thresholds for the large enterprise category during the year, this will not lead to the loss of the large enterprise status, unless it occurs in two consecutive accounting periods (EC Recommendation 2003/ 361 / EC, Art. 4 (2)). Consequently, if, according to the last two annual reports, the company should not be included in the list of large companies, the company will, if necessary, prove to the TTJA that it is classified as an SME".133 Also for multi-national companies, Estonia sticks to the SME Guide of the EU and makes it clear in the abovementioned guideline published by TTJA: "In the case of multinational companies, the economic status of the company's subsidiaries in other countries is used to determine the company's status (SME or not) according to the SME Guide." Regarding the energy audits performed for international companies, only the energy use of the parts of the company located in Estonia has to be audited. Only multinational s registered in Estonia can be identified in the list of obligated companies. 7.4 Information to enterprises (also via e.g., sectoral associations) about the obligation of Article 11(1) and Article 11(2) Under the EED 2018, the classification of non -SMEs needed to be made transparent to the companies to provide a clear picture on who has to carry out the audit. In the EED recast, it will remain important to offer information that describes obliged companies in a non -ambiguous manner and that clearly states all exceptions. Common queries can be covered by FAQ section, and general information can be provided in graphical leaflets. All the information regarding the obligation and changes to the obligation could be made available for the enterprises on a central information centre, ideally on the website of the national agency or any other external institution that acts as an information centre for businesses. Relevant keywords can ease the search for information, whilst links to external sources can provide additional information. 133 DEESME Task 2.2.: "Country template for the challenges - ESTONIA".

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 76 • Central storage of information materials (information hub) • Barrier free access • Relevant cross-links and keywords 7.6 Facilitating the self-declaration process For EED 2018, Bulgaria based its approach already on self-declaration. By 31 January of each year, all companies subject to the compulsory audits must submit a declaration to the agency in charge of Art. 8. of the EED 2018 using a template determined in the national legislation.140 The self-declaration process can be facilitated by providing detailed support material (e.g. FAQ or information document). In addition to p ublishing the requirements, information on the audit obligation must be communicated to companies that are likely to be subject to the obligation. This can be done, for example, by asking regional institutions to pass on the information, or by approaching trade associations. 7.7 Good practice examples for high quality energy audits Several good practice examples on quality aspects of energy audits are summarised in the DEESME report.141 On the quality of energy auditors, a good practice can be found in Austria, where the multitude of auditors was increased by qualifying auditors separately in different audit areas: b uildings, processes, and t ransport. By the end of December 2020, the publicly available list included 608 approved auditors. 110 were qualified in all three areas, 523 for buildings, 383 for processes and 153 for transport. In Denmark, the number of auditors was increased by cross-border accreditation. Energy auditors from neighbouring countries are also accepted to perform energy audits. Links to certified auditors are provided by the Danish Energy Agency. In Sweden, energy auditors have to pass a test with both written and practical parts in addition to required training and working experience. Germany requires energy auditors to take regular trainings. Every 2 years energy auditors are expected to complete 16 units of training, each 45 minutes. In Croatia, accreditation is valid for a period of seven years, and can then be reissued by meeting the national requirements again. The national authority in the Netherlands provides a Word template containing all necessary elements of the energy audit. This facilitates the reporting for auditors and enterprises. However, the use of this template is not compulsory. With the SEAI Energy Audit Handbook, Ireland created a 64 page interactive PDF as a step-by-step guide through the whole process of conducting energy audits and reporting of the results. Most countries allow the exclusion of certain parts of energy consumption. In Austria, all consumption areas (buildings, processes, transport) contributing to less than 10% of the total energy consumption may be excluded from the energy audit. As stated in the H2020 DEESME project, to increase the consideration of nonenergy benefits (NEBs), knowledge about the subject within companies , and especially individuals who provide energy advice, is essential. Furthermore, the consideration of NEBs can be enforced by integrating it in the national legislation as a mandatory aspect of energy audits, or by integrating the topic into the auditor curriculum. • Inform companies about NEBs: Raising awareness on the existence and relevance of NEBs is a key factor to increase the uptake of energy efficiency measures. • Enforce the integration of NEBs: The consideration of NEBs can be anchored as a mandatory element within the energy audits process or energy management system. 7.8.2 List of tools and projects related to multiple benefits Since the EU has acknowledged the role of multiple benefits of energy efficiency, CINEA has supported several projects focussing on this topic. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 80 8 Article 21 on basic contractual rights for heating, cooling and domestic hot water 8.1 Introduction Article 21 of the EED Recast aims at strengthening the position of consumers by introducing basic contractual rights for the supply of heating, cooling and domestic hot water, in line with the rights set out in Directive 2009/73/EG regarding the provision of gas services and Directive 2019/944 regarding the provision of electricity. Stakeholder involvement, including energy suppliers, consumer groups, and regulators, is crucial in the early stages of this transposition process to address specific challenges and national differences. In this report, we present the findings of an exhaustive analysis aimed at identifying good practice examples in accordance with the requirements of Article 21. Our research delved into the current practices across various countries, with a particular emphasis on supply of other forms of energy and industries closely related to the energy sector, such as the telecommunications sector. This choice of industries provided comparative data, allowing us to draw meaningful parallels and insights. Central to our investigation was an indepth examination of contract design. We scrutini sed how contracts are structured and communicated in these sectors, focusing on the transparency and accessibility of information for end customers. This aspect was critical in understanding how consumers interact with and understand the terms of their service agreements. Furthermore, our study paid special attention to the mechanisms in place for handling complaints and resolving disputes. By analysing how these industries manage customer grievances and disputes, we gained valuable perspectives on effective resolution strategies that prioritise fairness and customer satisfaction. Through this comprehensive approach, our report aims to offer actionable insights that align with the objectives of Directive 2023/1791 (in particular Article 21) related to energy efficiency. It serves as a synthesis of good practices from the gas, electricity, and telecommunications markets, highlighting innovative and effective practices in contract clarity, customer empowerment, and dispute resolution. 8.2 Transparency and clarity in contract terms In Germany, the implementation of the Directive 2019/944 through the amendment of the German Energy Industry Act ( Energiewirtschaftsgesetz, EnWG) has significantly enhanced consumer rights related to electricity billing, consumption determination, and contract terms. A key aspect of these reforms is the emphasis on transparency and consumer protection in energy contracts150: • Contract Formation: Energy suppliers are now required to conclude contracts with household customers in writing. This includes forms like letters, emails, or SMS, explicitly excluding oral or telephonic agreements. • Mandatory Contract Information: Contracts must now specify whether metering operations and their associated costs are included in the contract. They must also clearly state the exact 150 https://www.bundesnetzagentur.de/DE/Vportal/Energie/Vertragsarten/start.html

Additionally, they must mention the right to change suppliers swiftly and without charge. • Contract Summary: After contract conclusion, suppliers must provide a concise and easily understandable summary of key contract conditions, including price, potential bonuses, supply start date, cancellation period, and minimum contract duration. • Dynamic Electricity Tariffs151: For customers with an intelligent metering system, suppliers are obligated to offer a contract with dynamic tariffs, informing customers about the advantages and disadvantages of such tariffs. • Uniform Consumption Determinatio n Regulations : Suppliers can use the meter reading from the network operator/metering service provider, read it themselves, or ask the customer to read it. Estimates are only allowed in exceptional cases. • Mandatory Billing Information152: Bills must clearly highlight the total amount and due date. Suppliers must provide contact details for telephonic and electronic communication. The bill must separately list components like taxes, levies, network, and metering charges, including CO2 price costs in gas bills. Suppliers must explain the bill if requested by the customer. What makes Germany a good practice example? These measures demonstrate Germany's commitment to ensuring transparency and clarity in energy contracts, reflecting good practices in consumer protection and contract management in the energy sector. This is a particularly strong example because the regulator (the Federal Network Agency, Bundesnetzagentur, which is the German regulatory office for electricity, gas, telecommunications, post and railway markets) publishes information centrally, providing clarity not only for consumers but also for suppliers. This centralised publication of information ensures that all parties involved in the energy sector are well informed, leading to fairer and more transparent business practices. This approach exemplifies the objectives of Article 21, namely transparency, fairness and non-discrimination in the energy market. 8.3 Fairness and contract changes Sweden and Finland have created an exemplary legal framework that embodies these principles. • Good practices in Sweden153 • Advanced Communication of Pricing Changes: 154 Swedish regulations mandate that district heating suppliers notify their customers of any contract alterations, particularly in terms of pricing, well in advance. This protocol ensures that customers are not caught off guard and can make informed decisions about their energy contracts. • Customer Right to Negotiation:155 In Sweden, particularly in the case of district heating services, if a customer disagrees with an increased price, they have the right to request negotiations with their supplier. If the dispute remains unresolved after these negotiations, the customer has the option of requesting mediation from the District Heating Board. This process provides an additional layer of customer empowerment, ensuring that their concerns are adequately addressed, and that pricing remains fair and competitive. • Customer Right to Contract Termination:156 In Sweden, if a customer disagrees with the new contract terms, especially price hikes, he has the right to terminate the contract without incurring any penalties. This right empowers customers and ensures that energy suppliers maintain fair and competitive pricing. • Regulatory Oversight:157 The Swedish Energy Markets Inspectorate (Energimarknadsinspektionen) plays a crucial role in overseeing these practices, ensuring compliance with both national and EU regulations. • Good practices in Finland158 • Proactive Consumer Information:159 Finnish energy suppliers must notify consumers of changes in prices, charges, or other contract terms, including when these changes will take effect and the reasons for the changes. They are required to inform their customers proactively about any intended changes in contract terms. 160 This practice aligns with Article 21, emphasising customer awareness and the ability to make informed choices. • Change in Price Clause - Bilateral Application: 161 Finnish regulations ensure that the change in price clause in energy contracts works both ways. This means that just as suppliers can increase prices due to rising procurement costs, they are also obliged to reduce prices when their procurement costs decrease. This approach ensures a balanced application of rights and obligations between the parties, maintaining fairness in the c ontractual relationship. It prevents unilateral advantages and ensures that consumers benefit from decreases in energy procurement costs just as suppliers might benefit from increases. These practices in Finland demonstrate a commitment to fair and transparent energy market operations, closely aligned with the principles set forth in Article 21. • Contract Termination Rights:162 Similar to Sweden, Finnish consumers have the right to terminate their energy contracts without penalty if they disagree with the changes, particularly in pricing. Suppliers are required to inform consumers of this right and the notice period for termination. During the notice period, new terms or prices do not apply, unless the change is due to legislation or official rulings. This righ t is safeguarded even in practical scenarios where consumers might lack alternative suppliers, as Finnish law and regulatory bodies ensure fairness in pricing. This approach ensures a consumer -centric market where suppliers are motivated to keep prices fair and transparent. 156 https://www.ei.se/ei-in-english/district-heating/your-protection-as-a-district-heating-customer 157 https://www.ei.se/ei-in-english/district-heating/eis-supervision-regarding-district-heating 158 Finnish Consumer and Competition Authority (Kilpailuja kuluttajavirasto): www.kkv.fi. 159 https://www.kkv.fi/en/consumer-affairs/facts-and-advice-for-businesses/the-consumer-ombudsmans-guidelines/changes-in-contract-terms/ 160 https://www.kkv.fi/en/consumer-affairs/facts-and-advice-for-businesses/the-consumer-ombudsmans-guidelines/changes-in-contractterms/#2.3 161 https://www.kkv.fi/en/consumer-affairs/facts-and-advice-for-businesses/the-consumer-ombudsmans-guidelines/changes-in-contractterms/#2.2 162 https://www.kkv.fi/en/consumer-affairs/facts-and-advice-for-businesses/the-consumer-ombudsmans-guidelines/changes-in-contractterms/#2.2

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 83 • Consumer Protection Agency Role:163 The Finnish Consumer and Competition Authority (Kilpailuja kuluttajavirasto, FCCA) enforces these practices, providing an additional layer of protection for consumers and ensuring adherence to both Finnish law and EU directives. The FCCA ensures fair and efficient market performance, focusing on the development of affordable products and services that cater to different consumer needs. Specifically, the Consumer Ombudsman, working with the FCCA, enforce s compliance with consumer protection legislation, particularly concerning marketing and contract terms. This approach ensures a balanced relationship between consumers and companies. Additionally, the FCCA provides information and instructions to prevent problems and offers Consumer Advisory Services and the European Consumer Centre to help resolve disputes impartially, ensuring consumers receive the redress they are entitled to. What makes Sweden and Finland good practice examples? Comparing these practices to those in other EU Member States, it is evident that Sweden and Finland are at the forefront in ensuring fairness and transparency in contractual changes. These measures align well with the requirements of Article 21, particularly in promoting clear communication, contract clarity, and consumer protection. The practices in Sweden and Finland offer valuable insights and a framework that Member States could emulate to enhance fairness in pricing and contract changes. These practices not only align with EU directives but also contribute significantly to consumer satisfaction and market efficiency. 8.4 Non-discriminatory payment methods The importance of nondiscriminatory payment practices in consumer markets, particularly in strategic sectors such as telecommunications and energy, cannot be overstated. This example looks at the French approach to such practices and shows how they comply with EU directives, in particular with Article 21(4) and the broader EU framework on consumer rights and payment services. The French approach offers valuable insights into ensuring fairness and inclusivity in payment practices, and enhancing consumer experiences. • Diverse Payment Options: French energy providers, in particular EDF (Électricité de France), offer multiple payment methods in their general terms and conditions , including online transactions, direct debit, credit card payments, and cheques .164 This variety ensures that customers with different financial situations and preferences have suitable payment options. • In France, as in other EU member states, regulations ensure equal treatment for all payment methods. Under the EU's Payment Services Directive ( PSD2), in particular Article 62, payment service providers are only allowed to charge fees in certa in scenarios, in line with the directive's provisions. This ensures that fees are reasonable and reflect actual costs. In addition, within the EU, payers and payees will each bear the fees of their respective payment service providers. Article 62 also limits the charges that a payee can levy for using certain payment instruments, ensuring that they do not exceed the direct costs incurred. This framework is part of a wider effort across the EU to promote fair, transparent and non-discriminatory financial practices. What makes EDF a good practice example? • When it comes to payment methods for energy services in France, suppliers such as EDF offer a variety of options that ensure compliance with both national regulations and EU directives such as PSD2. EDF's flexible payment terms, as detailed in its clause, are in line with the principle of non-discrimination in payment methods. Customers can choose to pay by direct debit, TIP (Titre Interbancaire de Paiement), cheque or credit card, and can even change payment method during the contract. This flexibility is further enhanced by the option of making equal monthly payments by direct debit, which facilitates financial planning and budgeting. EDF's approach reflects a commitment to fair and transparent payment practices, offering consumers choices that suit their financial circumstances, while complying with EU-wide standards of fairness and transparency in financial transactions. This ensures that consumers are not unduly penalised or restricted in their payment options, thereby promoting a consumer-friendly environment in the energy sector. 8.5 Accessible complaint procedures Ireland provides a notable example of good practice in accessible complaints procedures for energy services. The country has established a comprehensive and easily accessible framework for customers to complain about their energy contracts. The suppliers offer transparent information and specific "Code of Practice" on their websites which outline the standards of service that consumers can expect from the supplier in case of a complaint. This approach is in line with the spirit of Article 21, which advocates the protection of consumer rights through efficient complaint handling mechanisms. • Features of Irish complaints procedures:165 • Ease of access: 166 Customers can easily access complaint procedures through various channels, including online platforms, telephone and postal services. This multi -channel approach ensures inclusivity and convenience. • Timely resolution: Irish regulations require a timely response to complaints, in line with the Directive's emphasis on prompt and fair resolutions. This reduces potential stress and inconvenience for consumers. • Transparency: The process is transparent, with clear guidelines on how complaints will be handled and the expected timeframe for resolution. This transparency fosters consumer confidence. • Independent oversight: An independent regulator oversees the complaints process to ensure fairness and impartiality. This is in line with the Directive's requirement for independent enforcement of consumer protection measures. • Supplier education: 167 The Irish regulator published the "Electricity and Gas Suppliers’ Handbook".
