This enables consumers to understand their rights and the mechanisms available for redress. • Practical Implementation in Ireland • In Ireland, the complaint procedures for energy consumers are structured as follows: • Initial Complaint: Consumers first address their issues through the complaint process of their energy supplier or network operator.168 • Service and Timelines: Suppliers are e xpected to acknowledge and resolve complaints swiftly, with complex issues potentially taking longer. The Code of Practice, available on suppliers’ websites, details the complaint handling process, including resolution timelines.169 • Escalation to CRU: 170 Unresolved complaints can be escalated to the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) for further action. What makes Ireland a good practice example? Ireland's approach to implementing accessible complaints procedures in the energy sector is particularly notable for its information approach. The key to its success is effective communication, with clear and accessible information that enables consumers to understand and exercise their rights. This transparency in the complaint handling process, with clearly defined guidelines and timelines, significantly increases consumer confidence. The role of the CRU as an independent regulator adds a layer of fairness and impartiality in line with EU standards for consumer protection. In addition, the efficiency and accessibility of complaint channels underlines Ireland's commitment to consumer-centred practices. In summary, Ireland's approach to managing and communic ating regulatory information sets a commendable standard for consumer protection within the EU. 8.6 Barrier-free access to services Ireland's approach, particularly when it comes to vulnerable customers, stands out as one of the few examples of good practice in the European Union. This example looks at the key features of accessible energy services in Ireland and analyses what makes it a good practice model to ensure barrier-free access to energy services as a fundamental consumer right. • Key Features of Ireland's Barrier-Free Access • Definition and Identification of Vulnerable Customers: 171 Ireland's regulator, the CRU, provides examples on who could be seen as vulnerable customer. This registration is mandatory to avail of the additional protections and is designed to be free and straightforward, ensuring ease of access. • Additional Protection for Registered Customers: Once registered, these customers receive extra protection measures. These include specific rules on how suppliers must treat and communicate with them, as well as enhanced protection against disconnection for nonpayment. • Support and Accessibility Measures: 173 Energy providers like SSE Airtricity have taken proactive steps to support vulnerable customers. They maintain registers for prioritised service and offer options for a nominated contact to aid in account communications, ensuring that customers with different needs receive appropriate support. What makes Ireland a good practice example? Ireland's approach to ensuring barrier -free access to energy services for vulnerable customers is exemplary and has several key aspects that align well with Article 21. The country's methodology is comprehensive and inclusive, effectively covering all necessary aspects from the identification of vulnerable customers to the provision of the necessary safeguards. This ensures that no customer is left behind in accessing essential energy services, which is a crucial aspect of ensuring the rights of all consumers. In addition, the emphasis on clarity and transparency in communications by both regulators and energy suppliers such as SSE Airtricity is a great strength. This clarity ensures that customers are well informed about their rights and the services available to them, which is crucial to empowering consumers and improving their experience. The practices in Ireland can be a model for the implementation of Article 21, as it emphasises fairness, transparency and non -discrimination in the provision of energy services. This alignment not only demonstrates Ireland's commitment to EU standards, but also its desire to maintain high standards of consumer protection. In addition, the adaptability and customer -focused services offered by energy suppliers are particularly noteworthy. The flexibility in adapting services to the different needs of vulnerable customers underlines the commitment to accessibility and inclusiv ity and ensures that energy services are available to all citizens, regardless of their particular circumstances. While the implementation of these measures in Ireland sets a high standard, it is important to note that there appears to be room for improvement in all EU Member States. There are relatively few examples of good practice like Ireland. This suggests that i ncreased efforts and initiatives are needed across the EU to ensure that all Member States adopt and implement similarly comprehensive, inclusive and transparent practices. 8.7 Service Quality Assurance Quality of service in the Austrian energy sector is characterised by a comprehensive set of regulations that set high standards for energy suppliers. The country has established a solid regulatory framework, led by the 2010 Federal Electricity Industry and Organisation Act, which underlines its commitment to providing high quality electricity at competitive prices. This legislation aims not only to ensure fair and transparent market practices, but also to develop renewable energy sources, reflecting Austria's commitment to both consumer rights and environmental sustainability. The requirement for distribution system operators (DSOs) to publish terms and conditions approved by the E-Control Commission is evidence of Austria's insistence on standardisation and fairness in the energy market. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 90 Stromversnelling addresses a highly specified target group. The organisation focused previously on social housing associations, with mostly single-family buildings and a smaller number of apartment blocks. Working with these associations ensured a constant stream of contracts. The focus has changed to the owners of single-family buildings. Furthermore, Stromversnelling focuses on older buildings, due to their lower energy efficiency and correspondingly higher energy bills. Aradippou OSS (Cyprus, active since 2018, launched by a municipality) provides energy home renovation services to SFH. It does not directly interfere in the market, but matches different local stakeholders (e.g. private construction companies, energy auditors, financial institutions, etc.) with customers who are willing to engage in energy efficiency improvement or renovation projects.188 It has set up a local buildings registry, which allows to monitor renovation projects in the municipality. It also offers a range of different services such as energy audits, technical advice and postrenovation monitoring. However, customers are responsible for selecting and contracting with renovation professionals and financial institutions when applying for a loan. With regards to the financing of renovation projects, customers can benefit from a municipal tax deduction and a grant which depends on the amount of G HG saved by the project. The O SS services are free of charge, hence the OSS does not generate any revenues. It was originally set up through the Horizon 2020 project with a budget of around EUR 200 000 for three years. Future annual running costs of the OSS will be covered by municipal budget. Frederikshavn OSS (Denmark, active since 2017, launched by a municipality) is a public -private partnership that has been established to provide support to homeowners for their energy renovations. The municipality has selected a lead private partner through a public procurement procedure.189 The selected partner (Energiehuset) acts as the main contact point for homeowners and works in collaboration with various local stakeholders. The municipality also supervises and monitors the renovation projects led by the OSS. The OSS provides a wide range of services (raising awareness, energy renovation and financial plans, coordination of renovation projects, quality management) and is responsible for contracting with renovation professionals. Therefore, the customer only signs one contract with the OSS for its renovation project. Frederikshavn OSS does not provide financial products itself but has negotiated attractive conditions with local banks.190 The municipality does not finance the OSS (apart from a lump-sum payment at the kick-start of the OSS) and generates revenues through fees paid by customers. These fees are calculated as a percentage of the total costs of the renovation project (i.e. 5% for SFH and 10 to 15% for multi - family homes). The remaining part of the fees is paid to suppliers. Riga Energy Agency (Latvia, active since 2018, launched by a municipality) aims to provide all information on renovation programmes that are co-financed by the city of Riga and other actors.191 The OSS has physical offices located in the Riga Energy Agency that are open to customers twice a week. It provides awareness raising and information services on potential energy and financial savings as well as how to increase the value of a building. The OSS subcontracts another company for performing energy audits, which are financed by the municipality (80%) and by customers (20%). Based on the results of the energy audit, the OSS provides recommendations on how to improve energy efficiency of the housing. It provides information on the funding possibilities and supports customers’ application for the municipal subsidy scheme. The OSS is entirely funded by Riga City Council and does not generate any revenues. 188 Aradippou_INNOVATE-case-study_2020-en.pdf (energy-cities.eu) 189 Frederikshavn_INNOVATE-case-study_2020-en.pdf (energy-cities.eu) 190 Frederikshavn_INNOVATE-case-study_2020-en.pdf (energy-cities.eu) 191 Riga-Energy-Agency_INNOVATE-case-study_2020-en.pdf (energy-cities.eu)

It maintains contact with its customers throughout the entire process. A key strength of Operene is the provision of expert advice, for example, by providing an economic analysis of renovation options on a building level and the drawing up of sophisticated financing options.192 A key aspect of the service provided by Klimatfastigheter Småland AB (Sweden, active since 2019, startup) is their strong customer -oriented support, the ability to coordinate the entire renovation project and quality assurance approach.193 This company works with a network of key local partners. This ensures a reliable revenue source for the partnering companies as well as a n independent quality assurance of their work conducted by Klimatfastigheter. Furthermore, Klimatfastigheter collaborates with a large local energy provider. All partners are certified to improve the quality of the renovations. The strong focus on high quality is arising through Klimatfastigheter guaranteeing a standard to its customers.194 Reimarkt (Netherlands, active since 2014, private) also cooperates closely with smaller local companies. The appro ach is to match the renovations with the offers of partner companies. Furthermore, Reimarkt also offers financing options to its customers , which are operated directly through the OSS. 195 Customers can compose their own renovation project (onor offline) as Reimarkt connects their products and services directly with suppliers and related costs.196 The OSS has achieved an important conversion rate (i.e. percentage of customers reaching the implementation stage) of 80%. Customers pay a fee of approximately 10% of the total renovation costs, which consists of the main revenue stream of the OSS. Among the six OSSs, five also benefit from public support. BetterHome (Denmark, active since 2014, industrial partners) relies on standardised renovation packages to improve indo or climate and energy performance. BetterHome has established a network of local partners who have received training and were examined to ensure the service quality. These partners are coordinated by BetterHome and offer all services for the renovation of a building, including financing options. 197 A key characteristic of BetterHome is that it is a cooperation of four major Danish companies. The OSS generates revenues by taking a fee from installers in exchange for marketing, advice and coordination services providing them with value.199 In the long term, the OSS aims to become self-sufficient rather than relying on public support. Linneaus University OSS (Sweden, active since 2020, private) is a project that was initiated by a university in collaboration with various public and private stakeholders (including the municipality of Växjö).200 A startup called Klimatfastigheter Smaland AB is running the OSS and is supported by the university. The business model chosen by the OSS is one in which customers sign a single contract with the OSS, which assumes all risks and responsibilities. The OSS does not provide financing solutions, so customers must arrange their own alternatives. Revenues are composed of a fee charged to customers and of discounts negotiated with suppliers. Services offered by the OSS include information and awareness raising , energy audits/in spections, advices and recommendations on energy efficiency improvements, energy renovation and financial plan development, material and services quality assurance and management. Extremadura Region Energy Agency or AGENEX (Spain, active since 2020, launched by local public authorities) has set up an OSS, called OSIR, which acts as a single point of contact for customers (both single-family and multi -family homes) to provide advice and support on deep renovation projects.201 AGENEX and the regional government have both financially supported the development costs of OSIR. The main feature of OSIR is that it has set up a new incentive for banks, which consists of a guarantee fund allowing banks to offer more attractive loans to customers who are willing to engage in home renovation, with interest rates below current levels and 12 to 15 years of loan maturity. In addition, the OSS implement information campaigns, engages in energy audits and feasibility studies and contracts with suppliers (customers sign a single contract with OSIR). It does not perform post-renovation monitoring and quality assurance as this task is left to the ‘Works Direction body” in Spain. However, OSIR agrees with supplier of a certain expected energy savings target. If this target is not achieved, the OSS can retain a fee from the supplier. 9.5 ESCO-type model Oktave (France, active since 2014, semi-public company) has a strong customer focus and manages all steps required for a renovation project . It also offers post-renovation services for two years. In organising renovation works, Oktave assesses the needs and financial capacity of customers to develop renovation options and match them with companies carrying out the work. Furthermore, Oktave cooperates with local authorities, energy service companies and banks. In addition to these services, Oktave develops a financial plan based on a consideration of different funding sources. The provision of the services described is facilitated by cooperation with various partners. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 93 financial assistance.203 It proposes two different business models. In the first one, customers and the OSS collaborate to develop the plan and arrange the financing of energy efficiency measures, but the customer is responsible for the implementation. In the second one, the OSS provides a complete package of services; it develops the financial and implementation plan, provides third - party financing (through loans from the bank or from Ile -de-France Energies itself), supports in accessing other types of grants and acts as an intermediary between the owners and professionals.204 Customers pay a monthly fee for the project and the services provided by the OSS, taking into account energy savings. In addition, the monthly fee partly serves to reimburse the loans. The average Internal Rate of Return achieved by supported projects reaches 4 to 9% over 15 to 20 years. 9.6 Horizontal good practices Pre-fabricated technical elements: Employing such multifunctional prefabricated elements (e.g. prefabricated facades, insulated rooftops with solar panels, smart heating, and ventilation and cooling installations) results in a reliable quality and an increase in the effectiveness of the construction works, which in turn reduces costs and tenant disturbances. Through these methods the Energiesprong approach achieves net zero energy renovations.205 Combination with other refurbishment aims and partnership with transaction companies for the right timing: The usage of key moments contributes to the realisation of renovations. This includes moments when the building is newly sold or rented, as tenants are more likely at these times to invest in the property. Reimarkt specialised in this approach and established arrangements with real estate agents who offer their services to future tenants or owners. These offers are further enhanced in their attractiveness by combining different elements such as energy efficiency and comfort.206 Digitalisation: Digital tools are commonly used by OSSs. For example, Reimarkt and BetterHome conduct a pre -project phase in which the initial planning is conducted digitally. This helps customers develop their goals for the renovations and decide what is affordable for them. The tool proposes an optimised approach for the works , which is important for the implementation. This approach can also be used by the relevant bank to assess the project and facilitate the process of receiving a grant.207 Packaging of interventions and follow -up: To simplify processes, Reimarkt and BetterHome recommend specific packages consisting of different renovation measures. BetterHome also offers follow-up work to these packages and regularly promotes these to customers with a finalised renovation.208 Despite the significant practical value of digital tools, having a physical store location for an OSS is meaningful, as it can increase engagement.209 The balance here is key. OSSs are tools to reduce barriers to building renovations and digital and face-to-face offerings make distinct, yet synergistic contributions to this. Focusing on one aspect risks not realising the full potential of the OSS. With regards to rural environments, highly digitalised OSSs might offer significant advantages. 203 jrc113301_jrc113301_reportononestopshop_2017_v12_pubsy_science_for_policy_.pdf (europa.eu) 204 jrc113301_jrc113301_reportononestopshop_2017_v12_pubsy_science_for_policy_.pdf (europa.eu) 205 JRC (2021), One-stop shops for residential building energy renovation in the EU 206 JRC (2021), One-stop shops for residential building energy renovation in the EU 207 JRC (2021), One-stop shops for residential building energy renovation in the EU 208 JRC (2021), One-stop shops for residential building energy renovation in the EU 209 INNOVATE_guide_final.pdf (energy-cities.eu)

text: Fraunhofer ISI | 94 Pooling of buildings210: OSSs have different ways available to them to achieve economies of scale. With regards to smaller renovation works, buildings undergoing the same works can be grouped. In the case of deep renovations , developing standardised measures for similar buildings can be effective, as EnergieSprong exemplifies. The multi-disciplinary team of complementary actors is setup (i.e. architects and designers, constructors, energy -efficiency experts, market and financial experts, technology suppliers, strategy and operations planners) and works together from the initial design phase in collaboration with the building owner. “Step-by-Step” approach 211: When pursuing this approach, building parts (e.g. windows, plasterwork, roof covering, boiler etc.) are only exchanged when their life-span approaches its end. This allows to reduce the amount of works that have to be done during one instance and enhances their economic attractiveness. At the outset of such a renovation, however, a comprehensive plan could be developed, including for those measures which will be carried out several years in the future. In this way , a certain outcome regarding costeffectiveness, energy efficiency and quality can be guaranteed. An example for following this method is the OSS EnerPHit. Financial instruments212: Several OSSs provide financial services as part of their offer or act as intermediary for other actors (e.g. financial institutions), on which customers can rely for finding financing solutions. As financing is crucial f or t he implementation of the renovation services proposed by the OSS, relationships with financial institutions and other financial actors must be well-developed and maintained. There are a variety of financing instruments that can be used to support energy renovation, among which: 9.6.1 Private financing models 1) Energy Performance Contracting (EnPC) – This model is often followed by OSSs which initiated their business as Energy Service Company (ESCOs). Generally, the costs for the renovation are recuperated over time via the energy bill of the customer. Two sub-models exist. Firstly, shared savings, where the contractor receives a percentage of the financial savings achieved through the renovation. Alternatively, payments are done following the first out model, which means that the contractor receives the entire savings until the renovations are paid. An alternative name for this model is on -bill financing model, which is employed by the OSS Ile-de-France Energies (formerly Energies Posit'if). 2) Referred bank loans – An OSS with an established partnership with a bank has the possibility to give advice regarding the most appropriate financing options and support the process of obtaining funding. In this model, a regional or local authority that is linked to the OSS is not involved with its own resources in the financial products. However, other ways of interacting with actors offering funding is possible, such as training or other engagement. An example for this approach is BetterHome which has established cooperations with local banks, and engages in mutual training to facilitate the renovations. 9.6.2 Public financing models 1) Financial instruments & investment funds – An OSS that is related to public authorities may have access to public funds. This enables the offering of financial products on favourable terms to its customers. The possible origin of these funds are diverse and include direct borrowing 210 JRC (2021), One-stop shops for residential building energy renovation in the EU 211 JRC (2021), One-stop shops for residential building energy renovation in the EU 212 JRC (2021), One-stop shops for residential building energy renovation in the EU .

Such European funding may also be used to issue securities to local banks which in turn finance the renovation works. This model is often pursued by OSSs in France. 2) State aid - With regards to national funding, OSSs may benefit from the relaxing of State aid rules through the recent amendment of the General Block Exemption Regulation (GBER). The provisions contained in Article 38(b) and 39 are particularly relevant in this context. 213 More specifically, Article 38(b) sets out that entities offering energy performance contracting, as defined in Article 2(29) of the EED recast, are eligible for State aid under eased conditions. In consequence, only those OSSs which offer energy performance contracting are eligible. This entails the provision of energy efficiency improvement measures as well as a contractually agreed level of energy efficiency improvement or other agreed energy performance criterion. Therefore, OSSs from the all -inclusive model and ESCOtype OSSs are favoured by State aid rules. Coordination model OSSs may also fall withi n its scope in certain cir cumstances, whilst the facilitation model will generally be excluded. 3) Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) – This model represents the most direct involvement of public bodies. For example, a local government issues bonds which are used to finance the renovation. The repayment is being done through an increase on the property tax. This financing method emerged in the United States and has been tested through the EuroPACE project. Additionally, the Horizon 2020 project INNOVATE has developed a list of relevant lessons learnt for renovation OSSs which may be considered and which are summarised below.214 213 European Commission (2023). text: Fraunhofer ISI | 96 Getting people on board: • It might take a lot of time before first results of the one-stop-shop are visible. • It is important to take time for local stakeholders and homeowners. • Local suppliers might not be able to meet the OSS’ quality criteria. Setting up the OSS: • It is important to consider the geographical location, size and attractiveness of the territory. • An online platform is a must to increase the one-stop-shop efficiency and conversion rates. • It could be interesting to opt for a neighbourhood approach in energy renovation. Financing the OSS: • If available, use subsidies to develop infrastructure and partnerships. • If the OSS is a private company or a cooperative, try to obtain support from local or regional authorities on your area of operation. • Consider alternative revenue sources for the OSS, in addition to service fees charged to homeowners Financing to homeowners: • The OSS could offer innovative services to the citizens. • The OSS can facilitate project bundling and act as an interface vis-à-vis financial institutions. Engaging homeowners: • Get ‘real’ marketers and salespeople on board.

topic: good practices for the energy efficiency directive
text: Fraunhofer ISI | 97 10 Article 24 on empowering and protecting vulnerable customers and alleviating energy poverty 10.1 Introduction Article 24 of the EED Recast creates a new obligation for Member States to take appropriate measures to empower and protect people affected by energy poverty, vulnerable customers, lowincome households and, where applicable, people living in social housing. This chapter presents good practices related to ringfencing budgets and offering higher subsidy levels to low-income or vulnerable households. It brings examples on supporting landlords of rented buildings and capacity buildings for the intervening specialists. 10.2 Mitigation of distributional effects from other policies and measures 10.2.1 What are distributional effects? The distributional effects of policies and measures are crucial to take into consideration when designing them, as this will determine how different segments of the population, in particular households or individuals of different income levels, are impacted. Anticipating these impacts is crucial for proactively addressing potential disparities and inequities resulting from the implementation of policies. This is important to enable policymakers to design and implement policies and measures that promote a more just and inclusive society. Negative distributional impacts: Negative distributional impacts occur when policies and measures disproportionately affect people in energy poverty, vulnerable customers, low -income households and, where applicable, people living in social housing215. For example, policies that lead to price increases in essential goods and services, such as energy, can have regressive effects. Low-income households, which spend a larger proportion of their income on these necessities, bear a heavier burden compared to higher-income households216. This can deepen poverty and perpetuate income di sparities, widening the gap between the rich and the poor. Positive distributional Impacts: On the contrary, policies and measures that benefit the listed vulnerable groups can be considered as positive or progressive 217. Such policies and measures frequently encompass targeted social programmes, income transfers, or measures aimed to enhance access to essential services for this target group. A range of policies and measures are used by Member States to mitigate distributional effects, including structural tax ref orms, financial payments or cashback, investments in technology or equipment at the individual/household level, or investments in public service/infrastructure to 215 Pizer, W. A., & Sexton, S. (2019). The distributional impacts of energy taxes. Review of Environmental Economics and Policy. 216 Neuhoff, K., Bach, S., Diekmann, J., Beznoska, M., & El-Laboudy, T. (2013). Distributional effects of energy transition: impacts of renewable electricity support in Germany. Economics of Energy & Environmental Policy, 2(1), 41 -54. 217 Cabrita, J., Demetriades, S., & Fóti, K. (2021). Distributional impacts of climate policies in Europe.

title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
topic: good practices for the energy efficiency directive
text: Fraunhofer ISI | 98 benefit the most burdened groups or communities. Investments in energy efficiency measures at the household level, as targeted by Article 24 of the recast EED, and in some cases in public services and infrastructure, are particularly relevant to help mitigate negative distributional impacts of policies and measures that increase energy bills or other energy -related burdens. Whereas measures to increase income or help to pay energy bills provide support only in the year they are offered, energy efficiency investments provide more sustainable solutions and help to address the structural inequalities that lead to the negative distributional impacts, like inefficient homes and access to only expensive, inefficient, or polluting energy sources218 . To support the assessment of distributional impacts , the Commission provided Guidance in 2022 (COM/2022/494) on better assessing the distributional impact of Member States policies219 . 10.2.2 Energy Efficiency Obligation Scheme The Energy Efficiency Obligation Scheme (EEOS) in Ireland 220 is an ongoing programme administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) that obligates energy suppliers and distributors to deliver energy savings. Under the EEOS, the obligated parties have specific targets that can be reached by offering support and incentives to improve the energy efficiency of homes and businesses. F or each unit of energy saved, obligated parties earn energy credits that count towards their targets. All energy types, including electricity, gas, and solid fuel, are included in the scheme. Launched in 2014, the scheme has undergone revisions and upd ates, including an increase in residential deemed credits. What makes the energy efficiency obligation scheme a good practice? The Energy Efficiency Obligation Scheme (EEOS) acknowledges that energy costs can place a disproportionate burden on low -income households. By means of ‘ringfencing’ the scheme allocates a minimum percentage of 5% of the total energy savings to the benefit of low-income or vulnerable households. This mechanism addresses the impact of the costs being passed on to customer bills and promotes energy saving measures being implemented as a priority for low - income or vuln erable households. The prioritisation of e nergy savings measures allows these households to reduce energy bills, increase indoor comfort, and improve energy affordability. So, the EEOS effectively reduces the energy burden and promotes equitable access to efficient energy resources for all citizens. The implementation of Energy Efficiency Obligation Schemes (EEOS) in various Member States has demonstrated a pattern of gradual introduction, learning, and redesign. In countries like Italy and Denmark, the schemes underwent a learning process before significant savings targets were established. However, new EEOS schemes offer opportunities to expedite the delivery of significant energy savings. One approach is to leverage the experience gained from existing voluntary schemes for obligated parties. Another option is to adopt and adapt successful EEOS designs from other countries, utilising their good practices and lessons learnt221. 218 OECD (2021). text: Fraunhofer ISI | 99 10.2.3 Financial assistance programme for homeowners "MaPrimeRénov Sérénité" in France 222 is a government programme aimed at promoting energy renovation and improving the energy efficiency of homes. Launched in 2020, the programme provides financial assistance to homeowners to undertake energy-saving renovations and upgrades in their properties. The programme offers a comprehensive support package, including financial aid, technical guidance, and assistance throughout the renovation process. The programme targets both in dividual homeowners and condominiums, with different funding options available depending on income level and the type of renovation. The financial aid provided through the programme is financed by energy suppliers as a way to fulfil their obligations under the Natio nal White Certificate or “Certificat d’Économie d’Énergie (CEE)”223 programme. What makes the financial assistance programme for homeowners a good practice? In response to the challenges faced by low-income households in accessing and affording energy savings upgrades, the "MaPrimeRénov Sérénité" programme incorporates various measures to address these challenges. One important aspect is the allocation of higher subsidy levels, in particular for low-income households, ensuring that they receive increased financial support. In addition, the National White Certificates Scheme aims to ensure that 25% of the White Certificates are generated to benefit low-income households. The programme also offers technical assistance throughout the renovation process and simplifies the application process, making it easier for vulnerable households to participate. These households are given priority access, ensuring they can benefit from the programme's resources. Additionally, "MaPrimeRénov Sérénité" provides information about other eligible funding schemes and collaborates with local authorities and community organi sations to establish a comprehensive support network. By combining ringfencing, higher subsidy levels for low -income households, and information measures, "MaPrimeRénov Sérénité" effectively supports and protects vulnerable groups. It strives to remove barriers, provide financial assistance, and ensure equita ble access to energy -saving measures for those who need it the most. As part of the broader strategy to optimi se energy consumption of energy poor households, MaPrimeRénov Sérénité is complemented by additional longterm initiatives that include educational programmes aimed to better promote energy usage practices within households. Additionally, direct income support measures are implemented to alleviate the burden of energy bills. Social tariffs, coupons, and energy cheques are among the initiatives designed to provide financial assistance specifically targeted at low -income households. These measures work in synergy with MaPrimeRénov Sérénité to address the multifaceted challenges faced by energy poor households, promoting sustainable energy practices and equitable access to energy resources224 . 222 MaPrimeRénov Sérénité .Consulted on 08/06/2023, more information . 223 Broc, J. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 100 10.3 Good practice on public funding - Home energy efficiency programme The Home Energy Efficiency Programmes for Scotland (HEEPS) 225 offer financial assistance and incentives to homeowners and tenants to make their properties more energy -efficient, reduce carbon emissions, and lower energy bills. HEEPS is primarily funded by the Scottish Gov ernment and implemented through various agencies and market actors such as local authorities and energy efficiency organisations. These entities collaborate closely with homeowners, providing guidance, evaluating eligibility, and administering funding and incentives to facilitate energy efficiency measures. The programme focuses on concrete measures to enhance energy efficiency, including insulation upgrades such as loft or cavity wall insulation, the installation of efficient heating systems like boilers or heat pumps, and the adoption of renewable energy technologies like solar panels. In addition to financial assistance, HEEPS provides energy advice and raises awareness on energy efficiency measures. It offers resources and information to homeowners, enabli ng them to understand energy efficiency options, reduce energy consumption, and make informed decisions about their homes. What makes the home energy efficiency programme a good practice? The Scottish HEEPS combine national funds for energy efficiency and heat with top-up funding for costly measures based on the local area, along with a zero-interest loan. The programmes include targeted schemes and initiatives for low -income and vulnerable households to tackle energy poverty and improve the energy efficiency of their homes. One of these schemes is the Warmer Homes Scotland programme226, which provides tailored support to eligible households. Warmer Homes Scotland offers free energy efficiency measures and improvements to eligible households, including insulation, heating system upgrades, and renewable energy installations. It is designed to make homes warmer, more comfortable, and more affordable to heat, particularly for those facing energy poverty. The HEEPS actively promote energy efficiency upgrades among landlo rds by offering them financial incentives, grants, and tailored support programmes specifically designed for rental properties. This approach effectively addresses the split incentives challenge that often arises when renovating buildings occupied by v ulnerable consumers, who are predominantly tenants. By incentivi sing landlords to invest in energy -saving measures, the HEEPS benefit both landlords and tenants. Landlords can take advantage of funding options and access resources provided through the HEEPS to enhance the energy efficiency of their rental properties, which may include insulation upgrades and the installation of energy-efficient heating systems. The Home Energy Efficiency Programme s for Scotland (HEEPS) have been successful in identifying and addressing barriers for renovation, making home improvements more accessible to a majority of consumers. Since its establishment in 2015, the Warmer Homes Scotland programme, a part of HEEPS, has had a significant impact by assisting almost 25 000 households in energy poverty. The programme is accompanied by a comprehensive evaluation method known as Social Return on Investment (SROI), which goes beyond financial measures to recogni se the broader value created by the programme . Among the value created, 79% is attributed to households who directly benefit from the programme's initiatives227. 10.4 Good practice on network of experts - Energy poverty observatory The National Energy Poverty Observatory (Observatoire National de la Précarité Energétique or ONPE)228 was created in France in 2011 as part of the implementation of the Grenelle 2 law (n°2010788 du 12 juillet 2010). The ONPE serves as a national initiative to monitor, analyse, and combat energy poverty. The establishment of the ONPE was a response to France's commitment to sustainable development and the need to address the challenges of energy poverty. The primary objective of the ONPE is to collect accurate and widely shared information about energy poverty in France, with a specific focus on the housing sector and mobility. The primary goals of the ONPE are to provide a comprehensive and reliable perspective by producing accurate, consistent, and comparable data on both the phenomenon of energy poverty and the measures and financial assistance aimed to prevent and mitigate its impact. The ONPE also s erves as a platform for stakeholders to engage in national discussions, offering recommendations and proposals to address energy poverty. Furthermore, the ONPE plays a crucial role in sharing and raising awareness of its research findings through its regularly updated website, publications, dashboard, and diverse events. The ONPE's expertise has also served as a reference for the establishment of energy observatories in other countries such as Spain or Italy. What makes the energy poverty observatory a good practice? The ONPE brings together a range of professionals from various disciplines, including researchers, academics, policymakers, energy providers, social organisations, and other relevant actors. This is an important factor that contributes to the success of the network. The ONPE's network of experts enables the sharing of knowledge, experiences, and good practices related to energy poverty and provides decision -making support to government services, agencies, associations of energy suppliers and local authorities among others. The information is shared in a comprehensive way which facilitates its outreach to the general public. This structure enables the ONPE to bring expert advice and data-driven evidence to local and regional entities that are near vulnerable groups. This approach allows for a multidisciplinary approach that helps to understand and identify successful practices to tackle energy poverty in France229. From an organi sational perspective, the ONPE is supported by the French Agency f or Ecological Transition (ADEME)230, which is responsible for managing the secretariat and coordinating activities in collaboration with partners. The ONPE functions as a dynamic entity that addresses significant transition challenges by facilitating various working groups (WG). These working groups, including both permanent and ad hoc groups, play a crucial role in monitoring the ONPE's work. There are four permanent working groups. The Household-WG conducts surveys and research to understand the impact of e nergy poverty on households. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 103 11 Article 26 on heating and cooling supply 11.1 Introduction Article 26 addresses various aspects of decarbonising heating and cooling (H&C) supply. The main emphasis of this chapter is on district heating and cooling ( DHC) systems. Best practices are presented to support Member States in implementing the following aspects: • Voluntary use of labelling efficient DHC; • Linked increases of energy efficiency and usage of renewable energy; • Innovative approaches to developing DHC systems; • Integrated approaches to expanding DHC systems and energy efficiency; • Phasing out coal use in DHC systems; • Furthermore, three approaches to the calculation of the GHG emissions from (high-efficiency) cogeneration are presented. Lastly, the chapter goes into best practices for the conduct of costbenefit analyses (CBA) of various installations. 11.2 Voluntary uses of district heating labelling Articles 26(1) and 26(2) provide a definition of efficient DHC (EDHC) systems. The good practices presented in this section aim to present examples of Member States that have created labels to reflect the efficiency of DHC systems. The primary use of such labelling is to facilitate the administration of financial support. Other effects include stimulating competition between DHC operators and informing customers about the activities of their heating and cooling suppliers. This would be achieved through the publication of the labelling data, as being done in France and the Czech Republic. 11.2.1 Annual and public surveying of DHC systems The French district heating and cooling association FEDENE, representing public and private operators, and the union SNCU conduct an annual survey on DHC systems. 231 This survey is mandatory for all of the 898 DHC systems in France and collects data on various technical and business-related aspects. This survey establishes a high-quality database with which the regulator is able to further develop the relevant legislation. For example, DHC systems above a certain carbon footprint are prohibited. It is also the basis for the threshold for a DHC system to be classified as efficient or ‘virtuous’ (vertueux). To obtain this rating under French law, the following criteria must be met:232 • At least 50% renewable or waste heat; • Metering per point of delivery; • The DHC system’s operation reaches a certain level of profit within a defined period of time (i.e. the depreciation period). 231 FEDENE (2023), Enquête annuelle FEDENE Réseaux de chaleur & froid. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 104 For publicly-operated DHC systems, receiving t his classification is generally mandatory but there are exemptions. For private operators meeting the criteria and receiving the classification, is optional. However, it is highly attractive to obtain the classification for both operators and customers. Firstly, within a defined zone around a classified DHC system , it will be mandatory to connect new buildings and existing buildings that renovate their heating and/or cooling system. Consequently, operators benefit from a secured demand, which grants the necessary security for substantial investments.233 Secondly, for consumers being connected to a classified DHC system results in a reduced VAT rate paid on the supplied heating or cooling. The French government's website on DHC systems provides details of these procedures and regulations, together with documents to help operators fulfil their obligations or benefit from exemptions.234 11.2.2 Incentives for efficient DHC systems In Germany, the definition of efficient DHC systems established by the previous version of the EED has been integrated in several German laws. The primary criterion is that the DHC system operates with a high share of renewable or waste heat. This share varies between different policies. For existing networks, the establishment of a plan to reach emission neutrality by 2045 is another key component. Through this integration into the legislation, the operator itself or other actors may benefit from being classified as ‘efficient’. In general, this increases the financial security of the DHC system operator, which in turn enables the high investment cost for efficient DHCs. Examples of these mechanisms are: • The Building Energy Act (Gebäudeenergiegesetz), which obliges building owners to equip their building with heating and cooling systems that are operated with a certain share of renewable energy. However, instead of carrying out the necessary renovations to H&C systems, building owners can fulfil the obligation by connecting the building to an efficient DHC system. • The CHP Act (Kraft-Wärme Kopplungsgesetz) which provides that the operator of an efficient DHC system has the right to claim an additional charge from the TSO, directly increasing the revenue. • State aid regulations, such as the federal support for efficient buildings (Bundesförderung für effiziente Gebäude) which provides, among other measures, that buildings which receive a connection to a DHC system operated with a share of 65% of renewable energy can be supported. Specific to district heating networks is the federal support for efficient heating networks (Bundesförderung für effiziente Wärmenetze). Funding through this policy is only available to district heating networks which fulfil criteria in line with the definition of efficient DHC systems, as provided by the previous EED. In particular, the German policy requires that newly built DHC systems implement a variety of measures, such as the integration of renewable and waste heat, low temperatures and storages. For existing systems it is required that operators create a plan that results in emission neutrality until 2045. Every year, until the 30 April following an evaluation of requests, the Energy Regulator publishes a list of efficient DH systems. In the Czech Republic, efficient DHC systems are defined through the energy mix they have been supplied with in the previous calendar year. The reference values closely follow the previous EED.235 In order to be classified as efficient the operator must submit the necessary data to the national Energy Regulator who conducts the assessment and publishes a list of all efficient district heating systems.236 Compliance with the definition allows the DHC system to benefit from national funding, the height of which is dependent on the share of renewable heat in the network. Furthermore, the support is adjusted annually, based on the energy and operational costs borne by the operator. Through this system, the Czech government offers tailored support to operators of efficient DHC systems, based on the costs they incur. While this does not support high investment expenditure, as in other good practices, it does provide security for such investments. Furthermore, it protects operators from strong fluctuations in the price of different energy sources. 11.3 Good practices on the application of cost -benefit analysis requirement This section presents examples on how cost-benefit analysis (CBA) are conducted in practice. From a high-level perspective, the following points should be considered to optimise CBAs across different use cases: 7 • Cost underestimates are more common than overestimates and vice versa for benefits: • Often, two problems come together: costs are never overestimated and benefits never underestimated. For 80% of the sample benefit overrun did not outweigh costs overrun; • Data issues, e.g. benefits need to be quantified or related to life-time data; • Causes for flawed estimates are often optimistic assumptions about e.g. speed, costs, weather, or underestimation of negative influences and overestimation of mitigation measures; • Measures to increase accuracy include: • Establishing a large data set of similar projects with comprehensive data (e.g. reference class forecasting). Furthermore, SO WHAT offers trainings on their website, for optimal usage of the tool.240 11.3.2 Cost-benefit analyses for data centres Whilst the debates on capturing and utilising waste heat from data centres has been discussed in academic and business contexts for a number of years, it has become a new debate in policy - making. Therefore, good practice regulations on how to conduct cost-benefit analyses in this field need to be implemented. However, there are some governments which have already acted to encourage data centre operators to reclaim excess heat. These include Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Norway.241 Nevertheless, to provide guidance on the concrete aspects how to set up a framework for these cost-benefit analysis, it is necessary to consider academic literature. In general, there is consensus in the literature that data centres are a valua ble contribution to the heat transition. To carry out this assessment for a specific data centre , it is important to consider the following aspects: 1) Energy efficiency of the data centre itself: • Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) indicates the energy used by IT equipment. The closer it is to one, the greater the likelihood that the cost-benefit analysis will be negative; • Other energy efficiency indicators could be taken into account, for example, the Energy Reuse Efficiency (ERE). It is a measurement derived from the PUE and quantifies the amount of energy that is reused, generally outside of the DC. It is therefore a crucial indicator to establish the costs and benefits from reusing the waste heat of a DC.242 2) Employed cooling technology: • With liquid-based cooling waste heat can be captured more easily; • Quality of the heat; • Heat demand close to the data centre; • Investment costs; • Associated with the cooling technology; • Necessity of investing into a heat pump + operation/maintenance; • Design of the DC. Importantly, it is relevant to mention that DC operators in Stockholm stated that they are not capturing and selling waste heat primarily due to an economic motivation, as the efforts and additional cost outweigh the business opportunity.243 Instead, they are motivated through a social responsibility. In the short-term, this can be remedied by putting financial incentives, for example via tax reductions, in place. Furthermore, taking account of wider societal benefits, such as reduci ng emissions, may change the calculus. An example how this assessment can be automated, albeit in a different context, is a tool provided by the Danish Energy Agency for CBAs related to DHC systems.244 In the long-term, it could be that costs and effort decrease as technologies and procedures are developed which make this enable DC operators to derive a notable profit from selling waste heat. 11.3.3 Cost-benefit analyses for DHC systems As CBAs for DHC systems are not covered by the provisions of Article 26, in this section, we provide some valuable good practices and readily available tools which have been developed in different Member States. 11.3.4 In-depth CBA for DHC systems The city of Groningen conducted a very detailed CBA during the planning process of a DHC system.245 Practitioners can derive relevant information for conducting CBAs , in particular, regarding the following aspects: • Taking account of the wider benefits provided by DHC systems; • Necessary input data and creating scenarios for comparisons between different options; • Specification of key variables with either a strong or a weak influence on the balance between cost and benefits. This CBA distinguishes the consequences of investing into a DHC system at a very fine level of detail. For example, outputs are specified for a variety of groups, including the overall society within the defined geographical scope, the government, households and several economic actors (e.g. DHC system operators, heat producers, heat supplier s and actors who are indirectly affected through the DHC systems such as electricity providers and actors who are replaced through the DHC system). Furthermore, it considers a wide variety of actions next to constructing a DHC system, such as investing into building insulation and buildinglevel heat production. Consequently, the required input data is extensive. At an overarching level, it can be divided into the following categories: • Variables for policy options. This i ncludes data on the heat sources and the planned DHC system; • Variables to determine the scope of the analysis. This defines the boundary of the analysis and provides data on relevant aspects within the boundary such as type, number and energy consumption of buildings; • Input data for the CBA. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 110 actors can rely on readily available material and methodologies to prepare these inputs, by working in a resource-efficient manner. 11.4 Good practices on the calculation of GHG emissions from cogeneration installations According to Article 26 of the EED, Member States have to decide which approach they want to use to demonstrate EDHC. Either the approach based on the share of renewable energy or the emissions-based approach can be chosen. The calculation of emissions related to CHP installations, will be necessary for Member States if they opt for the EDHC definition that revolves approximately the emission intensity of the energy supplied to the network. Given the limited treatment of this procedure in the Guidance Note itself, in this report, it is further elaborated. There are two principal methods to determine greenhouse gas emissions from CHP plants: On one hand, direct measurements can be obtained through a continuous emissions monitoring system, while on the other hand, the analysis of fuel input is possible by calculating the carbon content in combusted fuel. A key challenge when calculating the emissions of a CHP installation arises through the circumstance that emissions may change , depending on the ratio of heat and power generation. In particular, when the generated heat and electricity are consumed by different users, an allocation of emissions to heat and electricity must be carried out. Multiple methods are available to conduct allocation of emissions. The following methods are used in the EU: • Energy method; • Alternative generation method; • Power bonus method; • Exergy method; • 200% method; • PAS 2050 method; • Dresden method; • Work method; • Finnish method; • All savings allocated to electricity or heat; • 50/50 sharing. In the EU project lowtemp.eu248, a multi -criteria analysis was performed in terms of popularity, thermodynamic aspects, data availability and sensitivity to identify the most suitable methods. The methods Exergy, PAS 2050, and the 200% method (in descending order) were rated as the best in the multicriteria analysis after A GFW, ZEBAU, BTU, RTU, IMP PAN, Thermopolis, and HEM. In the following, these methods are explained in more detail. 11.4.1 Exergy Method The exergy method, despite having more input parameters compared to other methods, is relatively simple to implement, as it uses directly measurable data. However, it has a limitation in that it does 248 LowTemp (2021). CO2 emission allocation in CHP systems and recommendations. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 111 not fully consider exergy losses caused by heat exchange during the cogeneration process. Nevertheless, the exergy method is considered a robust option for CO2 emission allocation in CHP systems, due to its ability to provide a more comprehensive understanding of energy quality and thermodynamics. The allocation of the CO2 emission relies on exergy content of electricity and heat. Exergy of electricity ExE equals produced power E (ExE = E). While the conversion of electricity into another form of energy can be 100% efficient, the conversion of heat typically involves losses. For heat exergy, ExQ applies: ExQ = (1-T0/ T) * Q where Q is the produced heat, T0 represents the average ambient temperature during the heating period and T is the thermodynamic mean temperature of the heating network. T can be calculated with the supply and return temperatures of the DH network Ts and Tr: T = (Ts – TR) ⁄ ln (T S/TR). For the CO2 allocation factor for heat production f Q, it holds fQ = ExQ / (ExQ + ExE) while the CO2 allocation factor for electricity production fE = 1 - fQ = ExE / (ExQ + ExE). Further information can be found in the following sources: Microsoft Word - Zertification_of_CO2_AK_EnEV_Robbi_Sander.doc (tu-dresden.de) https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1359431114010175 11.4.2 PAS 2050 Method This method is based on the process-specific ratio of heat to electricity for different cogeneration systems. The CO2 allocation factor for heat production is defined as f Q = Q /(Q + n * E) where n describes the emissions generated during the combustion of fuel , and indicates the additional amount of emissions from heat production that is allocated to the electricity. The factor n is typically 2.0 for turbine -based and 2.5 for boiler -based CHP systems. For the CO 2 allocation factor for electricity production applies: fE = 1 - fQ and fE = (n * E) / (Q + n * E). Due to the limited number of input parameters, this is a simple method. However, without a precise determination of the factor n, this method can be inaccurate. Additional details are located in the following source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1359431114010175 11.4.3 200% Method The fuel emissions are used to calculate the allocation of the CO2 emissions. In this method, it is assumed that heat production operates with 200% efficiency: To produce 1 unit of heat, 0.5 unit of fuel is needed. The remaining 0.5 unit is expected to be reclaimed from the turbine condenser. Consequently, half of the emissions associated with heat production can be attributed to power generation, which leads to the following formula: fQ = Q / 2 Fuelin where Fuelin is the total primary fuel energy consumed in the cogeneration plant. Furthermore, applies f E = 1 - fQ. This method enables the allocation of fuel costs in the energy and emission statistics. The 200% method is simple to implement but relies on an assumption that is not always realistic. The method assumes a constant heat production efficiency, which is chosen as a general average between the energy and exergy methods. Further details are available within the following reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1359431114010175 More information about various allocation methods can be found in the following sources: • Greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel fired power generation systems - Publications Office of the EU (europa.eu) • CO2 emission allocation (lowtemp.eu) • CHP Energy and Emissions Savings Calculator | US EPA

The main reason behind this is that the integr ation of renewable energy sources in district heating and cooling system s often allows to have lower temperatures, which inherently increases efficiency. 11.5.1 DHC system operating at 45°C-30°C In the town of Bjerringbro (Denmark), a local district heating network is using surplus heat from an industrial plant located in the city centre. 249 The surplus heat is extracted from a groundwater cooling system and is then boosted into a heat pump before it is fed into the network. A pilot study was conducted in order to assess whether it would be possible to use lower supply temperatures (of 45°C) in the local distri ct heating system and obtain higher heat pump efficiency.250 The study was conducted in a neighbourhood composed of around 20 single-family houses, in which domestic hot water substations with electric boosting were installed. While no other changes were made to the existing houses and their space heating systems, none of the inhabitants faced any issues to maintain thermal comfort into their houses. The network, which is normally operating at annual average supply and return temperatures of around 70°C/40°C, is now able to provide supply and return temperatures with an annual average in the range of 45°C/30°C. The central heat pump in the district heating system obtained COP - values ranging between 3.35 and 5.04. Due to the low heat density of the area, it was found that the district heating operation with lower temperatures would be favourable for the efficiency of the distribution network and would al so be economically viable due to availability of cheap surplus heat. 249 Euroheat & Power (2021), Ultra-low-temperature district heating in Bjerringbro, Denmark. As a result, a large renovation project took place between 2011 and 2015, combined with the (still ongoing) transition towards 4 th generation district heating. Thanks to the large number of stakeholders involved, the project was able to take advantage of some local subsidies and apply for various sources of funding. The houses were renovated with high insulation to reduce heating demand by 60% 268 and equipped with solar panels and PV supplying renewable heat and electricity.269 To supply the remaining heat necessary for space and water heating, the existing DHC pipes is being replaced with a low temperature DHC. Currently, there are more than 50 coal power plants producing heat for these installations. In total , they provide 81 TWh. 273 According to the BDEW, fossil fuels covered the vast majority of net heat production for DHC systems, with different coal types covering 20%.274 The coal phase-out at large and the replacement of coal as a fuel for DHC systems in Germany is being pursued through the interaction of several laws, most notably the Coal Phase -Out Act (Kohleausstiegsgesetz) and the Act for Nationwide Communal Heat Planning (Gesetz für eine flächendeckende kommunale Wärmeplanung).275 The former law stipulates that coal energy should be entirely phased out by 2038, whilst the latter law determines target values for the use of renewable and waste heat for DHC systems, up to climate neutrality for all DHC systems in 2045.276 Furthermore, it obliges local authorities to develop detailed H&C planning for their administrative district until 2026 or 2028, depending on the number of inhabitants. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 121 Based on this study, the process through which coal can be phased out and RES can be phased in efficiently could go through the following steps: • Establish heat supply planning and available heat sources on a highly localised level; • Replace coal wherever no significant adjustments need to be made to existing DHC systems; • Upgrade DHC systems to enable low temperature heat sources to feed into the grid. Secondly, the study discusses various policy measures which are divided into three categories, ‘planning, initiate and optimise the transition’; ‘decarbonise grids’; and ‘accompanying framework conditions’. In all categories, the study presents measures which are already implemented and further measures, for example: • Several financial support (planning, initiate and optimise the transition); • Public procurement programmes (decarbonise grids); • Price signals via the CO2 price (framework conditions); • Further measures can include a tax on fossil fuels and a reduction on the electricity tax. The flagship measure the German government has taken is the Ad Hoc Programme – Transformation District Heating ( Sofortprogramm zur Transformation der Fernwärme ), which provides financial support for a wide range of measures and contains public procurement contracts. Furthermore, it forms a triad with support programmes for the industry and buildings. DHC system operators have access to unbureaucratic support to address individual components of their DHC system. Under the requirement to develop a ‘transformation plan’ for existing grids, operators can access further funding for DHC system-wide measures, including demand-side actions. 11.8.2 Phase out of fossil fuels in DHC systems through heat planning Denmark is well-known for its heat planning strategies as a mean to move away from fossil fuels, amongst others, in the DHC sector. The oil crises of 1973 and 1979 had enormous impacts on Denmark, which was almost 100% energy import dependent in the 1970s. 278 These crises were a wake-up call for Danish authorities. In response, a legal framework was created with planning tools such as strategic H&C planning. 279 In the 1980s and 1990s, as environmental awareness and concerns were growing, the government published the first low-carbon energy transition strategy in the world. This pla n prioritised the integration of renewable energy sources into the energy system and planned for the phase-out of coal. It also included the finalisation of heat infrastructure planning initiated after the energy crisis. Heat planning was decentralised . In other words, local municipality councils had to ensure that future heating infrastructure projects were carried out in accordance with ministerial criteria. This would strengthen the integration of local ideas and initiatives in municipal heat planning practices, by increasing ownership of local heat planning. Figure 14 shows the evolution of primary energy resources in Danish DHC since the 1980s. The Danish DHC sector has integrated a large amount of renewable energy resources within a relatively short time period. text: Fraunhofer ISI | 125 12 Article 29 on energy services 12.1 Introduction Article 29 strengthens the promotion of energy services by the Member States . This chapter presents good practices on support schemes for energy services, their quality labels, pub lic guarantees, integration to other energy efficiency measures . It looks at the specific application in buildings renovations and at the monitoring of measures related to energy services. 12.1.1 Common terms related to energy services Energy services markets in Europe feature a variety of contract types, many types of contractors (suppliers) and a few types of clients from the public and private sector. Latter traditionally includes industrial companies or tertiary buildings. So far, both of the most common contract types, Energy Performance Contracting and Energy Supply Contracting have been applied in nearly all sectors, including also residential and SME. The following box summarises the most common terms with respect to energy services and provides an overview of the various forms of energy services used in different contexts in Europe.

title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
topic: good practices for the energy efficiency directive
text: Fraunhofer ISI | 126 Common terms related to energy services Energy Service means the physical benefit, utility or good derived from a combination of energy with energy-efficient technology or with action, which may include the operations, maintenance and control that are necessary to deliver the service on the basis of a contract and which under normal circumstances has proven to result in verifiable and measurable or estimable energy efficiency improvement or primary energy savings. Energy service provider is a natural or legal person who delivers energy services or other energy efficiency improvement measures in a final customer’s facility or premises. Performance-based energy services can be described as the general concept of an energy service, the quality of which is measured against a predefined performance guarantee. Energy efficiency service (EES): Agreed task or tasks designed to lead to an energy efficiency improvement and other agreed performance criteria. The EES shall include energy audits as well as identification, selection and implementation of actions and verification. A documented description of the proposed or agreed framework for the actions and the follow -up procedure shall be provided. The improvement of energy efficiency shall be measured and verified over a contractually defined period of time through contractually agreed methods [EN 15900:2010]. If the EES includes energy efficiency investments, it may or may not include financing of these investments. Partial services connected to energy efficiency services: Services that just include parts (“components”) of the EES value chain like design and implementation (excluding verification, for example), but that are designed to directly or indirectly lead to an energy efficiency improvement. If the partial EES includes EEI investments, it may or may not include financing of these investments. Energy performance contracting (E nPC) means a contractual arrangement between the beneficiary (or client) and the provider of an energy efficiency improvement measure, verified and monitored during the whole term of the contract, where investments (work, supply or service) in that measure are paid for in relation to a contractually agreed level of energy efficiency improvement or other agreed energy performance criterion, such as financial savings. A type of EnPC without major investments is sometimes called Operational Energy Contracting. Energy Supply Contracting (ESC) means a contractual arrangement for the efficient supply of energy. ESC is contracted and measured in Megawatt hours (MWh) delivered”. Integrated energy contracting (IEC) means a combination of energy efficiency measures with energy supply contracting typically with short term ‘operational verification’ rather than ongoing measurement and verification. Expanded energy service means a combination of EnPC with not only guaranteed cost savings from energy efficiency, but also from the provision of flexibility services. There is no clear definition, but according to Art. 29(4) such an extended energy service also includes demand response and energy storage services. Public private partnership (PPP) typically describes a long-term contractual arrangement for the provision of a public asset (such as energy efficiency investments) and related services (such as energy services) in exchange for performance-based payments linked to the asset’s availability and/or use and the delivery of the related services.

title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
topic: good practices for the energy efficiency directive
text: Fraunhofer ISI | 127 12.1.2 The (future) role of energy services in facilitating energy efficiency (and decarbonisation) investments On the way towards accelerating the energy transition, energy services can play a vital role by mobilising private capital for the investments at the consumer side. Energy services serve as an incentive for clients to engage in energy efficiency projects, allowin g them to shift organisational and, in some cases, financial burden to the service provider, the so-called Energy Service Company (ESCO). ESCOs have the necessary know-how to cover the whole service chain of energy efficiency projects, from choice of techn ology to installation and maintenance works. Especially, whe n providing Energy Performance Contracting, ESCOs additionally assume performance risks by linking their compensation to the performance of their implemented projects. This can be done through guaranteed savings, either when the customer takes over financing (financing is therefore on the clients’ balance sheet), or when the provider is responsible for financing being also the owner of the energy efficiency-related assets (off-balance sheet arrangement for the client). 12.1.3 Overview on the status and development of energy services markets in EU Member States The latest market analyses were conducted by the Joint Research Centre in 2019 and 2023.291 The reports describe the main market trends in the different Member States . As regards energy performance contracting (EnPC) markets, a general growth can be observed across Europe. In most Member States , the public sector as an EnPC customer is seen as a strong leader for market development of energy services. However, also the private sector is becoming increasingly important and even leads the market in a few Member States. A growing demand from private customers has been observed in nine Member States, i.e. Belgium, Cyprus, Finland, France, Hungary, Ireland, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia , whereas the public sector expanded, in particular in eight Member States, i.e. Belgium, Czech Republic, Slovenia, Austria, France, Greece, Germany and to a certain extent Hungary. In the next years, further growth is expected especially for private markets, whereas there is a risk that the public sector will lose momentum after leading the market's development. The clearest positive trends were forecast ed for eight Member States , i.e. Belgium, Czech Republic (especially in the public sector), France, Germany, Ireland, Poland, Slovenia (especially in the private sector), and Spain. Expectations for take-off were reported for three Member States , i.e. Romania, Sweden and Cyprus. Market contraction was only projected for Croatia (both public and private sectors). 12.2 Good practice examples The good practice examples presented in this chapter show how targeted policy instruments and programmes can have a decisive impact on the uptake of energy services in a Member State. In general, it is important that the selected policy mix aims both to stimulate the demand for energy services across all customer sectors (public, residential buildings, non -residential buildings, industry) and to improve the quality and quantity of supply of energy services through the ESCOs. Most of the following good practice examples directly refer to the requirements in Article 29 of the EED recast and are intended to provide suggestions on how a compliant transposition of Article 29 291 Moles-Grueso, S., Bertoldi, P., Boza-Kiss, B., Energy Performance Contracting in the EU 2020-2021, JRC Report, 2023, (https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/bitstream/JRC133984/JRC133984_01.pdf )and Boza-Kiss, B., Toleikyté, A., Bertoldi, P., Energy Service Market in the EU, JRC Report 2019 (https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/bitstream/JRC118815/jrc118815.pdf ).

topic: good practices for the energy efficiency directive
text: Fraunhofer ISI | 128 can have the best possible impact on the development of the energy service markets. In addition to these examples, we have selected a few other good practices – such as the Super-ESCO approach in Belgium or the different attempts to develop public payment guarantees f or energy services, which complement the mandatory policy measures under Art 29 and are likely to enhance the ir impact. 12.2.1 Public sector programmes and facilitation services Experience from several Member States shows that a surge in demand from the public sector can be decisive for the successful development of an energy service market . At the same time, it has become apparent that the public bodies predominantly have too little expertise in the field of energy services. Therefore, they need support facilitating the individual steps to be taken in the preparation and implementation of an energy service project. Among others, these facilitation services include the assessment of project suitability, the anal ysis of potential energy savings and investments required, support during the (public) procurement process including the preparation of tender materials, elaboration of contractual concepts, support in measurement and verification of energy savings during project implementation etc. The good practice examples presented below show different programme s to support the public sector. Some of these programmes, such as the Super-ESCO programme in Belgium, go beyond a straight facilitation programme and include direct implementation elements, while others, such as the Energy Contracting Support Scheme in Ireland, are available to both public and private customers. Local support facility: EOL in Slovenia The energy efficiency support facility “Energetska obnova Ljubljane” (EOL) has been one of the most successful projects funded through the ELENA facility of the European Investment Bank. The main achievement of EOL was the launch of two large tenders for E nPCs in the city of Ljubljana , retrofitting 76 public buildings (partly deep renovations), using an ESCO model. EOL has provided a range of services, including the identification of promising renovation projects, legal support for public procurement and public-private partnerships (PPP), technical assistance in terms of extended energy audits and energy monitoring as well as financial support for feasibility studies. Moreover, EOL had a significant impact on the market uptake of PPPs and EnPCs in Slovenia. At the start of the programme, there was a poorly developed ESCO market with no specific legal framework and no practice examples for PPP and E nPC projects. In cooperation with the relevant Ministries, official E nPC Guidelines have been developed in the course of the EOL programme , triggering a range of follow up projects292. FEDESCO as a Super-ESCO in Belgium A Super-ESCO can be described as an entity set up by public and/or private investors to provide full energy services, including financing, to its customers, subcontracting project implementation to private sector ESCOs that guarantee the expected savings. Super -ESCOs facilitate the identification of untapped opportunities for the use of energy services in specific target markets, such as the public sector, and, if well established, are perceived not as competitors to ESCOs but as facilitators of market development and growth. 292 Further information can be found in https://www.eib.org/attachments/documents/elena -completed-eol-en.pdf
